items.fullDescription: Poetry is a perfect medium to explore all of the key issues planned for the 58th Annual NeMLA Convention. The focus of this year's convention is Empowering Communities," which is identified on the NeMLA website as evoking the "process of transformation from a state of passivity to being active agents of change. It represents a shift away from authoritarianism and toward a model that values (and solves problems through) local knowledge, collaboration, and collective action," terms which lend themselves well to the emotional expressions within poetry. For the past five years, the Closet Poets sessions have enjoyed many scholars who research and write papers for conferences as well as write poetry. Perhaps those poems are jotted on note pads, in the margins of your papers or in dedicated personal journals. This session is seeking those scholars whose poetry often remains unpublished due to the heavier responsibility of publishing scholarly journal articles, monographs and genre-specific books which demand much time in between teaching, and perhaps, administrating at the university. Even though those scholarly efforts may yield more rewards, such as job retention and hopefully, job promotions; personal poetry, intermittently created, yields a satisfying venue for emotional issues and satisfying creativity. The 2027 Revisiting Closet Poets Creative session is an opportunity to expand and share your poetry by perhaps featuring the key issues of this years' convention. I am pleased to report that MLS published several participants poetic work since 2023 in their online venue. Perhaps you will have an opportunity to have your work published in MLS in future publications of our Closet Poets work. Remember the words of Poet Laureate, Robert Pinsky, who shared his joy of telling poems during a previous NeMLA conference, "Poetry is the breath of humankind, and must be heard." NOTE: This session is hybrid. It will be seated and accessible on Zoom. Please indicate which you prefer when you submit your proposals. Thank you. You do not need to be a NeMLA member to submit a proposal.

items.excerpt: This seminar proposes to approach William S. Burroughs not simply as a subject of study, but as a problem. We invite provocative papers grounded in comparative methodologies and attentive to less-travelled texts, episodes, affiliations, and cultural encounters. Rather than asking what Burroughs "was," we want to ask what his work does-and to pause over th...
items.fullDescription: This seminar proposes to approach William S. Burroughs not simply as a subject of study, but as a problem. We invite provocative papers grounded in comparative methodologies and attentive to less-travelled texts, episodes, affiliations, and cultural encounters. Rather than asking what Burroughs "was," we want to ask what his work does-and to pause over the categories through which we have learned to understand his oeuvre, asking what they illuminate and, perhaps more importantly, what they conceal. What notions of authorship, originality, literary value, sexuality, politics, nationality, identity, language, media, knowledge, or artistic production did Burroughs put under pressure? What happens when his writing is read alongside figures, traditions, media, or intellectual histories with which it is not usually associated? Can Burroughs's experiments still unsettle us? And what do we make of his political views today? We are interested in archival work, but not simply in the recovery of origins or the reconstruction of authorial intention. Archives can instead be approached as contested sites of selection, mediation, myth-making, and afterlife. We are equally interested in familiar Burroughsian techniques-cut-up, collage, montage, sampling, recording-when they are placed in unexpected comparative contexts. What do these techniques actually do? How have they travelled beyond Burroughs? How are they being used today, and by whom? We also welcome papers willing to be unfriendly to their subject. Is Burroughs overrated? Is he politically embarrassing, historically compromised, or aesthetically exhausted? Is he already "cancelled"-or has cancellation itself become another way of making cultural icons safe? Can Burroughs be restored, and if so, to what? Or is he damaged beyond repair? What might we gain by taking seriously the possibility that some of his work should be rejected rather than rescued? Possible approaches include, but are not limited to: Burroughs and writers, artists, or intellectual traditions with which he is rarely compared Burroughs and competing theories of authorship, originality, and literary value Archives, censorship, canonization, and the production of literary authority Burroughs and the politics of race, gender, sexuality, class, empire, and nationality Burroughs's relationship to religion, esotericism, anthropology, science, medicine, and alternative forms of knowledge Literary and non-literary media: sound, film, photography, visual art, performance, television, and digital culture Adaptation, appropriation, influence, imitation, and misreading The contemporary uses and abuses of Burroughs Critical reception, including hostile, skeptical, and revisionist readings We especially welcome proposals that are comparative in more than name: papers that put Burroughs into genuine friction with another author, tradition, medium, language, archive, or conceptual framework. We are less interested in proving that Burroughs anticipated everything than in discovering where he fails, contradicts himself, becomes strange, becomes ordinary, or becomes impossible to classify.

items.fullDescription: Call for Proposals Transformative Synergies Harmonizing the Future: Interdisciplinary Pathways for a Resilient Society Transformative Synergies brings together faculty, scholars, graduate students and practitioners to explore how disciplines can intersect to address the complex challenges shaping our world. As technology, public health, social policy, education and the arts continue to evolve, meaningful solutions increasingly require collaboration across traditional academic boundaries. This conference invites researchers and creators to examine the connections among arts, business, STEM, health and education and consider how these fields can work together to build a more resilient society. Submit Your Work We welcome proposals that explore innovative ideas, research and creative approaches related to the conference theme, including: Pedagogy for a New Era: Interdisciplinary curriculum design, trauma-informed education and the future of the R2 research institution Creative Technologies: Digital preservation, emerging technologies and the ethics of the human-machine interface Social Equity & Policy: Research addressing systemic health and educational disparities Health-Arts Nexus: Narrative medicine, art therapy and the role of the humanities in public health Sustainability & STEM: Environmental science, Indigenous knowledge and resilient urban design These topics are not exhaustive. Proposals that explore meaningful connections across disciplines are encouraged. Graduate Student Symposium The conference will feature a Graduate Student Panel designed to give emerging scholars an opportunity to share research in progress, completed projects, theses and dissertations. The session will provide a supportive environment for scholarly feedback, interdisciplinary dialogue and networking with scholars from across institutions. Proposal Formats We welcome: Individual papers Panel discussions Poster presentations Creative and multimedia works Workshops and interactive sessions Who Should Submit? Graduate students, faculty, researchers and practitioners from all disciplines are encouraged to submit original work that engages with the conference theme. Proposal Guidelines Proposals should be 300-600 words, depending on disciplinary standards, and address: Title - A concise, descriptive title that engages an interdisciplinary audience. Purpose and Central Question/Problem - The primary aim of the work. Conceptual, Theoretical or Disciplinary Framework - The intellectual foundation of the work. Methods, Materials or Creative Approach - How the work was conducted or developed. Findings, Claims or Scholarly Contribution - The work's intellectual contribution. Interdisciplinary Significance and Broader Impact - The relevance of the work beyond a single discipline. For panels, submit an individual abstract for each paper. How Proposals Are Reviewed All proposals will undergo peer review and will be evaluated based on: Clarity and coherence Scholarly rigor Methodological or interpretive soundness Originality and contribution to knowledge Interdisciplinary engagement and accessibility Relevance to the conference theme Conference Information Nov. 8-10, 2026 The Hotel at the University of Maryland Discounted rates are available for conference attendees. Ready to Contribute? Share your research, scholarship or creative work with an interdisciplinary community exploring new approaches to the challenges of the 21st century. items.fullDescription: CALL FOR PAPERS / COLLEGE ENGLISH ASSOCIATION ANNUAL CONFERENCE APRIL 1-3, 2027 / ST LOUIS, MO SUBMISSION SITE IS OPEN: https://www.conftool.pro/cea2027 DEADLINE: 11/01/2026 For its 2027 annual conference,the College English Association (CEA) invites proposals for papers and panels that explore the theme of "Gateways" and their significance in literature, criticism, and pedagogy. we also encourage proposals on GENERAL TOPICS, including AMERICAN, BRITISH, AND WORLD LITERATURES. DON'T KNOW CEA? YOU SHOULD! In December 1938, a group of young academics attending the MLA convention in New York took on the biggest name in their field-the MLA. They chose to forge a new path by organizing into the College English Association and offering a voice to "the college English teachers of America." Their aim was to upend the scholar-teacher dynamic by recognizing teaching as paramount. Today, more than eight decades later, the CEA continues in that same spirit. At our core, we strive to meet these goals through two venues: our Annual CEA Conference and our journal, The CEA Critic. With over 400 active members and a collection of regional affiliates, the CEA welcomes teacher-scholars at all levels-from graduate students to emeritus faculty-who share our belief that teaching is central to who we are and what we do. CEA WELCOMES GRADUATE STUDENTS As always, the CEA extends a special invite to students pursuing a graduate degree, not only to attend the conference but to submit their presentations to the CEA Outstanding Graduate Student Paper competition. The award carries a grand prize of $250 and publication of the winning essay in the CEA's flagship journal, THE CEA CRITIC. NEW FOR 2027:UNDERGRADUATE ROUNDTABLES CEA invites undergraduates to enjoy the conference experience by sharing their work in flash-essay roundtable sessions. A flash essay is a highly condensed, high-impact presentation (typically 300-1000 words, or 2-5 minutes) that delivers core research findings, a specific argument, or a compelling narrative. During roundtable sessions, the speakers and audience engage in discussion with each other in more of an open conversation than in traditional panels. Learn more about roundtables here: https://cea-web.org/about-roundtables. LEARN MORE: https://cea-web.org/cea-2027-%2F-st-louis

items.title: Academic Freedom Now: Rights, Classrooms, and the Future of Democratic Knowledge
items.excerpt: This panel examines academic freedom not only as an individual right, but as a collective condition necessary for the production, circulation, and contestation of knowledge within democratic societies. In alignment with the theme of Empowering Communities, we consider how academic freedom enables communities-within and beyond the university-to participate...
items.fullDescription: This panel examines academic freedom not only as an individual right, but as a collective condition necessary for the production, circulation, and contestation of knowledge within democratic societies. In alignment with the theme of Empowering Communities, we consider how academic freedom enables communities-within and beyond the university-to participate in processes of inquiry, critique, and meaning-making. The panel is structured around three interconnected vantage points. First, it addresses academic freedom as a legal and institutional framework, tracing its historical development and examining contemporary challenges, including policy restrictions, political pressures, and shifts in governance. Second, it considers the classroom as a site where academic freedom is enacted, negotiated, and sometimes constrained, focusing on pedagogical practices that foster open dialogue, critical engagement, and the capacity to navigate disagreement. Third, it explores the future of academic freedom in a changing political and technological landscape, asking how institutions, educators, and communities might work to sustain and rebuild conditions for intellectual autonomy and democratic participation. Across these perspectives, the panel foregrounds the role of academic freedom in supporting not only scholarly inquiry, but also broader forms of social engagement and collective agency. Participants are invited to consider how academic freedom can be understood as a shared responsibility and an evolving practice, rather than a static or purely individual entitlement. Possible Topics• Academic freedom and democratic institutions • Legislative and policy challenges to higher education • The classroom as a space of risk, dialogue, and dissent • Student voice, participation, and vulnerability • Pedagogies of disagreement and difficult conversations • Academic labor, precarity, and speech constraints • Institutional governance and autonomy • Rebuilding trust in higher education • Academic freedom in digital and platformed environments • Global perspectives on academic freedom

items.fullDescription: Thomas Mann, who would have been 100 in 2025, left readers a number of critical challenges. For one, the coded way in which Mann writes about his most dangerous subjects (homosexuality; knowledge of German guilt) still can fool by a credulous reader, meanwhile his essentializing treatment of race, gender, ethnicity, and class is shockingly unabashed. Then, there is the problem of Mann's reversal of political attitudes as the Nazis drove him-the loyalest of native sons-from Germany. As a young reactionary during the First World War, Mann wrote Reflection of an Unpolitical Man, showing such sympathy with the German politics of expansion and aggression in it that he famously considers whether perhaps the sinking of the Lusitania was a reasonable price to pay for the special German destiny. In the aftermath of World War II, under pressure from his children, Mann publicly denounced the Third Reich. Today, he is widely celebrated as a champion of democracy and opponent of Nazism on the global stage. This panel invites responses to the many contradictions of Mann's personality, which permeate his novels, diaries, and essays with remarkable consistency. Responses need not attempt to resolve these discrepancies, but rather interpret them. How do you relate to Mann as an authorial figure? Are there works by him you find troubling but love anyway? This is an opportunity to practice approaching an author's style with sympathetic care and moral scrutiny in equal part. In addition to Mann's queerness and biraciality (both of which he handled with discomfiting ambivalence), topics mights include such Thomas Mann favorites as music, medicine, language, philosophy, and even cinematography. Comparisons with other authors, artists, and theorists also welcome.

items.fullDescription: Please consider submitting to the ACLA seminar titled "South-South Literary Relations and the Remaking of World Literature" by September 21, 2026 . You can submit your abstracts here: https://www.acla.org/cfp/70fe7418-c14a-468d-be1d-809e878f2e00/submit-paper/46d872df-9512-49a7-89f7-8bc710370693 Abstract from the ACLA CFP: Since the rise of World Literature as a major field of inquiry, discussions of literary circulation have often privileged routes that pass through metropolitan centers, emphasizing translation into dominant European languages, global publishing networks, and institutions located in the Global North. Yet literary works have long traveled through alternative circuits that connect regions of the Global South directly, producing histories of exchange that challenge center-periphery models of cultural transmission. This seminar invites papers that examine literary relationships among Africa, Asia, Latin America, the Caribbean, SWANA, Oceania, and other locations within the Global South. Such relationships may emerge through translation, political solidarity, migration, anti-colonial movements, publishing networks, educational institutions, shared aesthetic projects, or indirect forms of influence. They may also involve moments in which Northern institutions, languages, or markets facilitate, mediate, redirect, or constrain South-South encounters, raising questions about whether these exchanges can ever be understood as entirely autonomous. Rather than treating the Global South as a unified category, the seminar seeks to explore its internal heterogeneity, asymmetries of power, and competing visions of solidarity. How do texts travel between Southern contexts? What historical, linguistic, and political conditions make these encounters possible? What role do translators, publishers, periodicals, archives, and digital media play in creating or sustaining South-South literary networks? How might these circulations reshape concepts such as influence, comparison, translation, reception, or worldliness? We especially welcome papers that interrogate the implications of South-South literary exchange for the study of World Literature itself. If literary circulation is not exclusively organized through Northern centers, what alternative maps of World Literature become visible? Can South-South networks offer different ways of imagining literary value, canon formation, and global comparison? By foregrounding overlooked routes of circulation and exchange, this seminar aims to reconsider how World Literature is conceptualized and to illuminate the multiple worlds through which literature moves. Possible topics include, but are not limited to: South-South translation; comparative studies across the Global South; Cold War and Non-Aligned literary networks; postcolonial and decolonial approaches; migration and diaspora; publishing and periodical cultures; digital literary circulation; transregional modernisms; indigenous and vernacular exchanges; reception studies; archives of literary solidarity; and new theoretical approaches to World Literature.

items.excerpt: Transatlantic Connections and the 'Special Relationship[s]': BAAS Postgraduate Symposium, 2026 V&A East Storehouse, London 9th November In 1946, Winston Churchill declared the need for a "special relationship between the British Commonwealth and Empire and the United States" in order to maintain world diplomacy, citing our shared language and cultural val...
items.fullDescription: Transatlantic Connections and the 'Special Relationship[s]': BAAS Postgraduate Symposium, 2026 V&A East Storehouse, London 9th November In 1946, Winston Churchill declared the need for a "special relationship between the British Commonwealth and Empire and the United States" in order to maintain world diplomacy, citing our shared language and cultural values as connecting the two countries. Although this 'special relationship' has continually been called into question by scholars, there is undoubtedly a channel of cultural and political exchange between the US and the UK, as well as with other countries, which has become even more urgent for discussion in recent years. The 2026 BAAS Postgraduate Symposium invites proposals from postgraduate researchers at all levels and across all disciplines on the topic of Transatlantic Connections and the 'Special Relationship[s]'. By using the term 'Special Relationship[s]', we intend to explore the relationship between not only the US and the UK, but also between the US and other countries. We invite panels and individual papers on this theme and encourage you to interpret it as broadly as you wish, including any aspect of the US's transnational cultural, political and literary connections, influences or contrasts. We welcome contributions from all realms of American Studies, including, but not limited to: literature and film studies, postcolonial and decolonial analysis, science and visual culture, and urban and environmental history. As this year's symposium will be held at V&A East Storehouse, the site of the David Bowie Archive, we are particularly keen on hearing from scholars exploring the etymologically and culturally rich prefix of the term 'Transatlantic' itself. This one-day symposium will involve not only academic panel discussions, but other activities such as a career development session, an introduction to the archives at the Victoria and Albert Museum, and a keynote address by Professor Mark Ford. The intention is to foster a strong postgraduate community in American Studies and to learn from both our peers and from leaders in our field. The symposium will be catered, hosted primarily in-person at V&A East Storehouse, but with a digital attendance option for those only able to join online. There will be time in the day to explore V&A East Storehouse and the David Bowie Centre. V&A East Storehouse is a working museum store with a rich archive for students to use in their research. The building is designed to allow visitors to get closer to objects held in the V&A collections and to the work of the museum itself. We welcome the submission of individual papers as well as proposals for complete panels of three researchers. Applications from groups of three or four researchers for roundtable discussions are also welcome. For panel and roundtable proposals, please also include a statement of up to 200 words on the aims of the collective submission, alongside the individual papers. Papers should be around 15-20 minutes long , and roundtables will consist of five-minute introductions by each researcher followed by 45 minutes of discussion. Interdisciplinary paper, panel and roundtable proposals are encouraged. Suggested paper and roundtable topics include, but are not limited to: - Case studies or broader comparisons between literary texts from the US and other nations - Case studies or broader comparisons between films from the US and other nations - Comparative political or historical analyses concerning the US and other nations - Comparative economic, scientific or environmental analyses concerning the US and other nations. Although the symposium will centre on 'Transatlantic Connections', we welcome proposals making any transnational comparisons rooted in American Studies. We especially encourage researchers from across Europe and beyond to submit and attend, as part of ongoing efforts to expand the EAAS community of postgraduates. We want to make this symposium as accessible as possible; we will be working to ensure a relaxed academic environment and we encourage anyone attending to email us with any access needs. Bursaries will be available from BAAS on a limited basis for students requiring financial support for attendance. The deadline for submissions is? 15th September 2026 .?Please send proposals including a title, an abstract of no more than? 250 words ?and?a short biography of no more than 200 words ?to Claire Watt at?claire.watt@baas.ac.uk. If you have any questions about the symposium, big or small, please get in touch and we will be happy to help. We look forward to hearing from you!

items.title: The Poverty of Literature
items.excerpt: REMINDER: SEPTEMBER 22 SUBMISSION DEADLINE American Comparative Literature Association 2027 Annual Meeting University of Houston May 20-23 The Poverty of Literature Organizer: Gabriel Quigley, University of Victoria (gabrielquigley@uvic.ca) How does literature represent poverty? Is poverty available for representation? The title of this seminar is taken f...
items.fullDescription: REMINDER: SEPTEMBER 22 SUBMISSION DEADLINE American Comparative Literature Association 2027 Annual Meeting University of Houston May 20-23 The Poverty of Literature Organizer: Gabriel Quigley, University of Victoria (gabrielquigley@uvic.ca) How does literature represent poverty? Is poverty available for representation? The title of this seminar is taken from Marx's The Poverty of Philosophy, which, in turn, subverts Proudhon's The Philosophy of Poverty. In it, Marx critiques the approach taken by Proudhon and other anarchist, communist, or socialist "theoreticians" who assume that economic categories exist independently of history. According to Marx, "so long as they look for science and merely make systems, so long as they are at the beginning of the struggle, they see in poverty nothing but poverty, without seeing in it the revolutionary, subversive side, which will overthrow the old society." A similar critique might be leveled at today's writers and critics: when literature and literary criticism engage with poverty at all, do they merely reduce it to an ahistorical economic category? What forms of reification, alienation, and exploitation does the literary assumption that poverty is available for representation produce? This seminar asks what literature owes to people experiencing poverty. At a time when 847 million people live in extreme poverty-95% of whom are in the Global South-it seeks to bring together research on the representation, history, and ontological status of poverty. Unlike Marx's "theoreticians," who "see in poverty nothing but poverty," scholars analyzing poverty through other frameworks-such as ethical demand, affective complexity, geopolitical disparities, aesthetic fetishization, and state failure-are strongly encouraged to submit abstracts. Papers may respond to such questions as: how should poverty be represented, if at all? Beyond an economic category, can poverty be conceived as an aesthetic, metaphysical, or phenomenological category? How is the concept of poverty entangled with conceptions of lack, deprivation, or destitution? How does the global distribution of poverty reflect the ongoing injuries of imperialism, colonialism, neocolonialism, globalization, and ecological catastrophe? Possible topics: - Poverty and realism; poverty and genre - The ethics of speaking for the poor - Testimony, life writing, and first-person accounts of poverty - Poverty and racial capitalism - Postcolonial and decolonial frameworks for poverty - Poverty and ecological catastrophe; climate precarity - Poverty and intersectionality (race, gender, sexuality, disability) - "Poverty porn," sentimentality, and voyeurism - Working-class literature and labor - Poverty in the Global South; imperialism and uneven development - Urban and rural poverty as literary landscapes - Homelessness and houselessness - Poverty and the archive - Poverty and affect: shame, solidarity, rage - The literary canon and class; institutional gatekeeping - Austerity, welfare, and the state in literature - Migration, displacement, and border crossing - Literature and human rights - Poverty as aesthetic, metaphysical, or phenomenological category - Poverty and ontology; being, lack, and deprivation - Bare life and destitution ACLA Seminar Description can be accessed here: https://www.acla.org/seminar/63e1eb87-fe99-49c9-aac0-517ccf904102. ACLA Paper Submission link: https://www.acla.org/cfp/2b603883-5d9b-44ae-a485-c732ba80d4bf/submit-paper. Papers can be submitted until September 22, 2026 .

items.title: Beyond Hegemony: Masculinities in World and Comparative Literature
items.excerpt: This panel examines how literary and cultural texts from diverse global traditions imagine masculinity not merely as an individual identity but as a relational and communal practice. In an era marked by migration, political polarization, social fragmentation, environmental crisis, and renewed struggles for collective empowerment, narratives of masculinity...
items.fullDescription: This panel examines how literary and cultural texts from diverse global traditions imagine masculinity not merely as an individual identity but as a relational and communal practice. In an era marked by migration, political polarization, social fragmentation, environmental crisis, and renewed struggles for collective empowerment, narratives of masculinity have become central sites through which communities negotiate belonging, responsibility, vulnerability, and resistance. While dominant models of masculinity have often been associated with hierarchy, authority, nationalism, and exclusion, contemporary world literatures increasingly depict alternative masculinities grounded in care, ethical responsibility, emotional openness, solidarity, and collective survival. Such representations challenge inherited structures of power while opening new possibilities for community formation and social transformation. This panel invites comparative and transnational approaches that explore how literary texts, films, cultural narratives, and other expressive forms construct, critique, or reimagine masculinities within local and global communities. Particular attention may be given to how gender intersects with race, class, migration, coloniality, religion, ecology, technology, and cultural memory in shaping collective identities and practices of empowerment. Situated within the broader concerns of World Literature and Comparative Literature, this session seeks to foster dialogue across regions, languages, and traditions while investigating how masculinities participate in the creation-or disruption-of empowered communities. We welcome papers addressing, but not limited to: Comparative constructions of masculinity across world literatures Masculinity and migration, diaspora, or displacement Literary representations of fatherhood, mentorship, and communal responsibility Masculinities in Global South literatures Masculinity and environmental or ecological communities Masculinity, memory, and post-conflict reconstruction Queer and non-hegemonic masculinities in world literature Masculinity and cultural resistance under authoritarian regimes Masculinity, religion, and collective belonging Masculinity and affect in contemporary global fiction

items.fullDescription: Call for Chapters Proposals Submission Deadline: July 17, 2026 Full Chapters Due: October 30, 2026 Submission Date: October 30, 2026 Introduction This edited collection features scholarly voices with attention to horror in its transmedia representations, including film, literature, comics, art, branding, and more. Chapters give attention to the ways that fans take up the realities and ideas presented in horror, the affordances of the genre, and participation in this network of storytelling. The reactions of readers/viewers/fans, the decisions of creatives, the presentation of ideas within particular forms of media, and more form elements of the researched conversation in this volume. Objective This collection seeks to advance conversation about the theoretical functions of horror across media including notions of adaptation and literary/literacy-based choices in the work. This includes, but is not limited to, design structures, cultural influences, the role of lore, (re)considerations of the monstrous, embodiment in the genre, sub-genre considerations, and more. Target Audience This book is intended for academics in media, literacy, literature, communication, and interdisciplinary fields. Students enrolled in courses in these fields can benefit from this knowledge as they pursue courses of study and further academic work in these disciplines. Recommended Topics Emotional and Philosophical Reactions to Horror Media Themes and Interactions across Media Representations in the Genre Adaptation Processes/Decisions/Designs in Horror across Media Studies of Narrative and Response/Interpretation Recent Trends/Movements in Horror Theoretical Approaches to Horror Composition/Representation Analysis of Race, Gender, Class in Horror Considerations and Reconsiderations of the Monstrous Author/Creator Decisions and Purposes in the Genre/across Media Horror Character and Author/Director Studies Critical and Analytical Work on Embodiment in Horror Critical and Analytical Examinations of Cultural Stories in the Genre The Role of Lore/Mythology in Horror Studies of Writing/Creating Processes in the Genre Fandom Communities, Fan Fiction, Cosplay, and Other Responses Submission Procedure Researchers and practitioners are invited to submit on or before July 17, 2026, a chapter proposal of 1,000 to 2,000 words clearly explaining the mission and concerns of his or her proposed chapter. Authors will be notified by July 31, 2026 about the status of their proposals and sent chapter guidelines.Full chapters of a minimum of 10,000 words (word count includes references and related readings) are expected to be submitted by October 30, 2026, and all interested authors must consult the guidelines for manuscript submissions at https://www.igi-global.com/publish/contributor-resources/before-you-write/ prior to submission. All submitted chapters will be reviewed on a double-anonymized review basis. Contributors may also be requested to serve as reviewers for this project. Note: There are no submission or acceptance fees for manuscripts submitted to this book publication, Theory and Practice in Horror Transmedia Fandom and Creation. All manuscripts are accepted based on a double-anonymized peer review editorial process. All proposals should be submitted through the eEditorial Discovery® online submission manager. Publisher This book is scheduled to be published by IGI Global Scientific Publishing, an international academic publisher of the "Information Science Reference", "Medical Information Science Reference", "Business Science Reference", and "Engineering Science Reference" imprints. IGI Global Scientific Publishing specializes in publishing reference books, scholarly journals, and electronic databases featuring academic research on a variety of innovative topic areas including, but not limited to, education, social science, medicine and healthcare, business and management, information science and technology, engineering, public administration, library and information science, media and communication studies, and environmental science. For additional information regarding the publisher, please visit https://www.igi-global.com. This publication is anticipated to be released in 2027. Indexing Information for Prospective Authors IGI Global Scientific Publishing meets the criteria for inclusion in major indexing services such as Scopus; however, it is important to note that all indexing decisions are made independently by these services. IGI Global Scientific Publishing books are selectively indexed by the indexing organization after publication. Indexing cannot be guaranteed for any book prior to publication, and the indexing organization has complete control over the final selection and timeline. Important Dates July 17, 2026: Proposal Submission Deadline July 31, 2026: Notification of Acceptance October 30, 2026: Full Chapter Submission January 1, 2027: Review Results Returned February 12, 2027: Final Acceptance Notification February 26, 2027: Final Chapter Submission Inquiries Jason DeHart University of Tennessee Knoxville dehartjason33@gmail.com Classifications Education; Library and Information Science; Media and Communications; Social Sciences and Humanities

items.fullDescription: About the book: Human machine interfacing can be as simple as pressing a button or as complex and entangled (also entangling) as inserting a brain chip into the skull. science fiction. Humans with implants, prosthetic and hybrid humans with electronic and mechanical extensions are yet another level are no longer science fiction. Yet, human-machine interfacing has started long before the invention of these technologies. Machines did communicate with us and tell us about themselves even before chatbots were invented. The clanking of a hammer on the anvil tells us that it is old and dull. The whistle of a microwave tells us that dinner is ready. The process of interfacing is not a one-way process.

items.fullDescription: Folklore is having a moment in South Asian writing, and it isn't a nostalgic one. Novelists, poets, memoirists, playwrights, and graphic novelists across the region and its diaspora keep returning to myth, oral narrative, legend, and vernacular ritual, not to decorate their work with the past, but to think through the pressures of the present: ecological collapse, historical trauma, gendered violence, migration, and a digital, algorithmic world the old tales never anticipated and somehow still speak to.

items.fullDescription: What is the real difference between speaking with nature and speaking for it? Is eco-centric thought a universally shared ideology, or does it develop in reaction to historical, philosophical, and socio-cultural contexts? In what way do the fundamental principles of Indian ecology vary from prevailing Western structures? These essential inquiries delineate the parameters of Ramachandra Guha’s Speaking with Nature: The Origins of Indian Environmentalism (2024), which effectively contests the notion that environmentalism is a unidirectional phenomenon dictated by Western influence. This view posits that the rest of the world, particularly the Global South, lacks eco-conscious awareness because it is ‘too poor to be green’.

items.fullDescription: Popular Culture Association (PCA): Health, Humanities, and Popular Culture 2027 Conference, Boston, USA, March 24-27 2027 CFP DEADLINE FOR ABSTRACTS 31ST OCTOBER 2026 Travel Grant Applications due 15th November The mission of the Popular Culture Association is to promote the appreciation and study of popular culture, as well as to advance rigorous, interdisciplinary research that illuminates the complexity, significance, and impact of popular culture across time and around the globe. We welcome and amplify voices from diverse backgrounds, disciplines, and perspectives by creating spaces-both physical and virtual-for scholars, educators, creators, and enthusiasts to connect, share ideas, and engage in meaningful dialogue about popular culture. The Health, Humanities, and Popular Culture Area is excited to receive proposals for the 2027 Popular Culture and American Culture Association Conference in Boston, USA, March 24-27 2027. Proposal topics should fall within the realm of how health is represented in popular culture through the humanities lens (art, books, comics, journalism and news, cinema, music, theatre, television, etc…). We are interested in receiving papers linked to various related Health issues: drugs or narcotics and popular fiction; vaccinations and popular culture; mental health care and the humanities; and clinical care and the arts. For the 2027 conference we are particularly interested again in examining relationships between health and sustainability/biodiversity/climate change in media and popular culture. The WHO (2023) argued that: "Research shows that 3.6 billion people already live in areas highly susceptible to climate change. Between 2030 and 2050, climate change is expected to cause approximately 250 000 additional deaths per year, from undernutrition, malaria, diarrhoea and heat stress alone. The direct damage costs to health (excluding costs in health-determining sectors such as agriculture and water and sanitation) is estimated to be between US$ 2-4 billion per year by 2030. Areas with weak health infrastructure - mostly in developing countries - will be the least able to cope without assistance to prepare and respond. Reducing emissions of greenhouse gases through better transport, food and energy use choices can result in very large gains for health, particularly through reduced air pollution". (WHO, 2023: https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/climate-change-and-health) We therefore invite papers that discuss the key role of communications and media in representing the sustainability/biodiversity/climate change threat demonstrating ways in which its significance are presented or, alternatively, ways in which denial are discussed in popular cultural forms. What are the likely ways in which communications can shape our understanding of this important economic, political and social issue? Proposals should be 250-300 words and exhibit a clear connection between health and popular culture. Submission from current paid members will be accepted through the PCA website. Deadline is 31st October 2026. https://sites.google.com/view/2026pcaconference/call-for-papers

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers (submission deadline October 31, 2026) Fairy Tales Area, American Popular Culture Association Annual Conference, 2027 Boston, MA, March 24-27, 2027 The Fairy Tales Area of the Popular Culture Association invites proposals for individual papers, panels, and roundtables for the 2027 annual conference in Boston, MA, March 24-27. We welcome submissions on all aspects of fairy tales, wonder tales, folk narratives, and their afterlives in literature, film, television, digital media, visual culture, performance, education, gaming, and popular culture more broadly. Papers may address oral tradition, literary fairy tales, folklore collections, adaptations, retellings, reception, translation, theory, pedagogy, gender, race, class, disability, nationalism, childhood, religion, ecology, material culture, or transnational circulation. For the 2027 conference, the Fairy Tales Area is especially interested in submissions related to two featured topics: 1. Adaptation of Fairy Tales This topic invites papers on fairy-tale adaptation across historical periods, genres, and media. Possible approaches include, but are not limited to: • contemporary retellings of fairy tales in fiction, film, television, theater, comics, games, and digital media; • fairy-tale villains, monsters, anti-heroines, and sympathetic retellings of traditionally negative figures; • identity, reflection, self-authorship, trauma, agency, and transformation in fairy-tale adaptation; • adaptation as cultural critique, remediation, commercialization, or popular mythology; • fairy-tale motifs across national, linguistic, and media boundaries. 2. Vladimir Propp's Historical Roots of the Wondertale. Marking the publication of the first English translation of Vladimir Propp's Historical Roots of the Wondertale (Indiana University Press, 2025), the Fairy Tales Area invites papers that revisit this major work and consider its continuing relevance for fairy-tale studies, folklore, narratology, adaptation studies, etc. Topics include but are not limited to: • Propp's Historical Roots of the Wondertale in relation to ritual, initiation, kinship, magic, social transformation, and other social and cultural contexts; • uses of Historical Roots of the Wondertale for analyzing particular tales, tale types, motifs, characters, spaces, objects, or narrative functions; • applications of Propp's work to contemporary fairy-tale retellings, fantasy, film, television, animation, gaming, digital storytelling, and other forms of popular culture; • the relevance of Historical Roots of the Wondertale for studying adaptation or recontextualization of older wonder-tale in modern media; • the place of national wonder tales in international fairy-tale scholarship, including issues of translation, circulation, reception, and comparison; • theoretical and methodological reassessments of Propp's work, including comparisons between Morphology of the Folktale and Historical Roots of the Wondertale, Propp's place in structuralism, narratology, folklore studies, anthropology, literary studies, and popular culture analysis, or the strengths and limitations of his method. Submissions on other fairy-tale topics are also welcome. Additional possible topics include: • Afanasiev, the Grimms, Perrault, Basile, Andersen, and other collectors or authors; • oral tradition and literary fairy tales; • fairy tales in film, television, animation, and streaming media; • fairy tales, gender, and sexuality; • fairy tales and religion, ritual, myth, or magic; • fairy tales and pedagogy; • fairy tales in translation; • fairy tales, horror, fantasy, and speculative fiction; • fairy-tale spaces, objects, bodies, animals, and transformations. Besides the scholarly analyses of fairy tales, we may consider creative and artistic projects that engage with fairy-tale traditions, themes, narratives, and their contemporary reinterpretations. Please submit an abstract of approximately 250 words by October 31, 2026. Panel proposals should include a title and brief description of the panel, along with abstracts and bios for each participant. Scholars at all career stages, including graduate and undergraduate students, independent scholars, and international scholars, are welcome. For questions about the Fairy Tales Area, please contact Dr. Olena Leipnik, Fairy Tales Area Chair, PCA, at soc_ovl@shsu.edu

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers Taylor Swift & Swiftie Studies Southwest Popular / American Culture Association (SWPACA) 48th Annual Conference, February 17-20, 2027 Marriott Albuquerque Albuquerque, New Mexico https://swpaca.org Proposal submission deadline: October 31, 2026 Proposals for papers and panels are now being accepted for the 48th annual SWPACA conference. One of the nation's largest interdisciplinary academic conferences, SWPACA offers nearly 70 subject areas, each typically featuring multiple panels. For a full list of subject areas, area descriptions, and Area Chairs, please visit https://swpaca.org/subject-areas/. The Taylor Swift & Swiftie Studies area invites paper proposals on topics related to Taylor Swift and/or Swifties from multiple vantage points. Since her debut in 2006, Taylor Swift has become a fixture of popular culture. Her career has been marked by incredible record-breaking highs and infamous tabloid-fodder lows. Known for her sharp lyrics, her evolving cross-genre musical styles, and her dedicated, creative fanbase (the Swifties), Swift's influence has been noted within music, fashion, economics, politics, and other cultural spheres of power. As an interdisciplinary area, we invite papers from multiple perspectives and disciplines. Topics might include, but are not limited to: • Critical interpretations of Swift's lyrics, eras, and/or personas • Considerations of Taylor Swift and politics, feminisms, activism and social justice • Interrogations of Swift and gender, race, class, and other identities/identifications • Analyses of Swift's connections to business, law, psychology, philosophy or other academic disciplines • Arguments about fandom, belonging, relating, creating and other Swiftie concerns • Examples of Taylor Swift's pedagogical relevancy All proposals must be submitted through the conference's database at https://swpaca.org/app. For details on using the submission database and on the application process in general (including submitting proposals for roundtables and preformed panels), please see the FAQS & Resources tab on https://swpaca.org/. Individual proposals for 15-minute papers must include an abstract of approximately 200-500 words and a brief summary of 100 words or less. For information on how to submit a proposal for a multi-paper panel, please view the above FAQs & Resources link. The deadline for submissions is October 31, 2026. SWPACA offers monetary awards for the best graduate student papers in a variety of categories. Submissions of accepted, full papers are due January 1, 2026. More details are here: https://swpaca.org/graduate-student-paper-awards/. SWPACA also offers travel fellowships for undergraduate and graduate students as well as contingent faculty: https://swpaca.org/travel-awards-students-faculty/. Registration and travel information for the conference is available at https://swpaca.org/albuquerque-conference/. In addition, please check out the organization's peer-reviewed, scholarly journal, Dialogue: The Interdisciplinary Journal of Popular Culture and Pedagogy, at https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/dialogue/. If you have any questions about the Taylor Swift and Swiftie Studies area, please contact its Area Chair, Juliette Holder at jholder1@csustan.edu. If you have general questions about the conference, please contact us at support@swpaca.org, and a member of the executive team will get back to you. This will be a fully in-person conference. If you're looking for an online option to present your work, keep an eye out for details about the 2027 SWPACA Summer Salon, a completely virtual conference to take place in June 2027. We look forward to receiving your submissions!

items.fullDescription: The Routledge Handbook of Hip Hop and Sport, Culture, and Activism Call for Chapters Description: The Routledge Handbook of Hip Hop and Sport, Culture and Activism addresses the critical need for a comprehensive academic survey of Hip Hop's connection to sport as a preeminent sociological and political force among Millennials and Generation Z. This handbook maps the emerging critical terrain where Hip Hop intersects with the sports-industrial complex, digital activism, and the persistent structures of racial capitalism and white supremacy. As the culture enters its second half-century, it serves as an emergent space for self-expression and identity formation, both to hegemonic and counter-hegemonic ends. The leading objectives of this volume are to delineate how Hip Hop's relationship with sport provides narrative resources for youth to explore their social realities in the context of late-stage capitalism and its bedfellows: white supremacy and patriarchy. This handbook explores both the route and roots of Hip Hop expression through the lens of the African diaspora and the historical relationship between Black expressive history and social movements. This handbook is also interested in the ways in which Hip Hop's relationship with sport can be oriented both towards liberation and political conservatism, particularly in the context of Hip Hop's historical and presentist embrace of Donald Trump and his representative movements. This project aims to both engage Hip Hop's historical relationship with sports (professional and amateur) as well as its contemporary shifts,such as the institutionalization of breaking in the 2024 Olympics and the rise of representation activism in major sports leagues (NBA, NFL) that create new tensions between cultural authenticity and corporate appropriation. It is intended to define the current state of theory and establish a foundation for future scholarship across the interdisciplinary fields of hip-hop studies, sport management, and Africana studies. Since this project is a handbook and not an anthology, the chapter topics have already been pre-selected by the editors. However, we encourage submissions that engage the specific areas of expertise of each contributor, and the contributor is welcome to interpret the proposed topics according to their own research and experience. The targeted audience for this handbook are advanced high school students and undergraduates, so chapters should be written with this audience in mind. We invite abstract submissions from Hip Hop practitioners, sport sociologists, scholars, graduate students, postgraduate researchers, and early career researchers. Details for Submission: Abstracts of 250-300 words for the chapters listed below must be submitted by October 31st, 2026. Microsoft Word or PDF formats will be accepted. When submitting your abstract, please include your name, affiliation, email address, title of chapter, and short biography (100 words). Authors will be notified of their acceptance by November 30th, 2026. Full chapters of 4,000-6,000 words (including references) are due by April 30th, 2027. For further questions, contact Dr. Micah J. Dobson (mjdobson92@gmail.com ) and Dr. Tyler Bunzey (tylerbunzey@gmail.com). Table of Contents Section 1: Hip-Hop: A Cultural Politic Chapter 1: The Context of Hip-Hop's Roots and Routes in the Early 1970s Chapter 2: Political Movements that Impacted Hip-Hop's Foundation Chapter 3: Hip-Hop's Formal Political Movements like "Rock the Vote" Chapter 4: Hip-Hop and Moral Panic Section 2: Hip-Hop Generating Identity Chapter 5: Hip-Hop and Generational Identity in the "Post-Racial" Era Chapter 6: Obama, Neoliberalism, and Hip-Hop Mainstream Partisan Politics Chapter 7: From "FDT" to Kodak Black: Hip-Hop's Complicated Relationship with Trump Chapter 8: Hip-Hop and the Black Lives Matter Movement Chapter 9: "Alright" and Social Protests Against Police Brutality Section 3: Hip-Hop and the Sports-Industrial Complex Chapter 10: A History of the Relationship Between Hip-Hop and Sport Chapter 11: Subculture to Spectacle: The Evolution of Breaking and Olympic Institutionalization Chapter 12: Ice Cube, The Big Three, and Mogul "Activism" Chapter 13: Jay-Z and the Problematics of the Roc Nation-NFL Partnership Section 4: Representing: Hip-Hop and Sport Chapter 14: The Politics of Aesthetics: Street Fashion, the Tunnel Walk, and Racialized Pleasure Chapter 15: Generational Agency: From Michael Jordan's Brand to LeBron's "Representation Activism" Chapter 16: The WNBA and Queering Hip-Hop Aesthetics Chapter 17: Hip-Hop Dance as Art and Sport

items.fullDescription: Mythology in Contemporary Culture at the Annual Conference of the Popular Culture Association Boston Marriott Copley Place March 24-27, 2027 The Mythology in Contemporary Culture area is dedicated to exploring mythological stories, figures and themes from all cultures and historical periods in all areas of popular culture. The frequent appearance of mythological motifs in popular culture speaks to the notion that mythologies, far from being relics of the past, continue to have significance. Contemporary revisionings and reinterpretations of mythological elements reflect the attitudes of current culture. Movies, television, gaming, comics, graphic novels, traditional literature, visual arts, performing arts, politics, blogs-the list goes on--hold both explicit and implicit renderings of archetypes such as Athena, Thor, Kali, and Maui, and of mythological narratives such as those found in bodies of sacred literature, classical Greek tragedies, medieval Grail legends, and culture hero narratives to name only a few examples. Proposals that pertain to the general theme of Mythology in Contemporary Culture are welcome. Potential presenters seeking inspiration for a paper topic might reflect on mythological aspects trending in media and entertainment, political currents around the world, the many "-isms" that underlie discrimination of all kinds, or the mythological aspects of a specific place (such as Boston). We will consider proposals for individual papers and/or panels organized around a theme. Sessions are 90 minutes, typically with four presenters per session. Presentations should not exceed 15 minutes. All submissions must be made through the conference submission site https://pcaaca.org/page/submissionguidelines Potential presenters must be current, paid, members of the PCA to submit proposals for the conference.For individual papers, please submit a title and 100-250 word abstract. For themed paper sessions, each presenter should enter their own proposal; for a panel proposal, each presenter should submit individually and the panel chair should contact Lol Fow with the title and a brief description of the panel and the names of the presenters. Questions about the Mythology in Contemporary Culture area may be directed to the Area Chairs: Lol Fow, efow@bmcc.cuny.edu Kate Rittenhouse, earth2k8@mac.com Important Dates to Remember: • Database opens for Submissions - Aug. 1, 2026 • Early Bird Registration Begins - Aug. 1, 2026 • Deadline for Paper Proposals - Oct. 31, 2026 • Travel Grant Applications Due - Nov. 15, 2026 • Early Bird Registration Ends for Presenters - Dec. 31, 2026 • Travel Grant Decisions / Notifications - Dec. 31, 2026 • Regular Registration Begins for Presenters - Jan. 1, 2027 • Preliminary Program draft available - Jan. 6, 2027 • Regular Registration Ends for Presenters - Jan. 31, 2027 • Late Registration Starts for Presenters - Feb. 1, 2027 Those Presenters Not Registered by Feb. 15 Will be Dropped from the Program CONFERENCE IN BOSTON, MA - March 24-27, 2027

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers ESOTERICISM, OCCULTISM, AND MAGIC Southwest Popular / American Culture Association (SWPACA) 48th Annual Conference, February 17-20, 2027 Marriott Albuquerque Albuquerque, New Mexico https://swpaca.org Submissions open: September 1, 2026 Proposal submission deadline : October 31, 2026 Proposals for papers and panels are now being accepted for the 48th annual SWPACA conference. One of the nation's largest interdisciplinary academic conferences, SWPACA offers nearly 70 subject areas, each typically featuring multiple panels. For a full list of subject areas, area descriptions, and Area Chairs, please visit https://swpaca.org/subject-areas/. Esotericism, Occultism, and Magic invites proposals relating to magical worldviews, practices, and representations, as well as consciousness transformation, the preternatural, the paranormal, hidden meanings, the power of transmutation, and related phenomena. Characteristic methods, beliefs, perspectives, paradigms and techniques include: arcane symbolism, imagery, and aesthetics; unseen forces, spiritual intermediaries, invisible agencies, nonhuman intelligences; synchronous patterns, non-ordinary causation, and anomalous processes. Examples of ideas and systems include Hermeticism, Gnosticism, Sufism, Tantra, Rosicrucianism, Freemasonry, Satanism, witchcraft, sorcery, demonology, astrology, alchemy, yoga, shamanism, parapsychology, as well as psychic and paranormal phenomena, along with beliefs and practices relating to altered states of consciousness, overlapping with the study of mysticism and New Age spirituality, channeling, positive thinking, manifestation, reality shifting, the power of intention, numerology, guardian angels, and Ascended Masters. Esoteric, occult, and magical concepts, beliefs, and practices appear in every culture and civilization; contemporary media and popular culture have embraced them enthusiastically, yet at times have reacted against them. The impact of esotericism, occultism, and magic on genre formation/content and popular cultural perceptions has been profound. Their themes and tropes continue to become increasingly prevalent throughout all media of popular entertainment, including arts, music, literature, film, television, anime, comics and graphic novels, as well as being nearly ubiquitous throughout interactive gaming of all categories and genres. Beyond entertainment media, esoteric, occult, and magical concepts and content appear in online memes and frequently in fashion accessories and aesthetics. Their popularity continues to inspire and provoke a variety of conspiracisms in reaction, along with various fads, trends, moral panics, witch-hunts, witch-crazes, and conspiracy theories. Examples include demonic intelligences in "AI" chatbots, anti-occult-conspiracism in QAnon; adrenochrome confabulations, Illuminati paranoia, bloodline of the Holy Grail beliefs, Satanic Ritual Abuse scandals. All reactions to, and polemics against, esoteric, occult, and magical content in popular culture, as well as projections concerning its presence, are therefore also suitable topics for this Area, as are political, religious, secular, scientific, and scientistic receptions of esotericism, occultism, and magic, along with instrumentalization of related concepts, beliefs, and practices in propaganda, intelligence, and information warfare. Special themes and topics of interest proposed for 2027: EOM and time, chronology, and anachronism; concepts of the paranormal, preternatural, supernatural, anomalous, weird, etc; conspiracism, the occult state, conceptions of secret government, and esoteric espionage; lies, fakes, frauds, forgeries, counterfeits, duplicates, deception, disinformation, and propaganda; confabulation, fabrication, imitation, and simulation; boundaries of magic, mysticism, and technology; technoccultism, cybermagic, and cosmotechnics; magic and engineering; EOM and hacking; impossibility and Forteana; humor, parody, and satire; EOM and "influencers", EOM and the media; immediatism; consumerism and consumption in and of magic, and also magic as consumption and as commodity/commodifiable; EOM and economics; the bureaucratic occult; legal regulation of EOM; demographics in and of magic; EOM and the personality; EOM and/as genre; EOM and repetition, reproduction, genetics, heredity, ancestry, generational transmission, generational trauma; EOM and radicalism; values, virtues, ethics, and empathy in EOM; EOM and geography, geopolitics, astropolitics, and "space"; egregores; crowd magic, "mass magic", and EOM-concepts of "the masses"; EOM and the mundane/banal; EOM and materialist worldviews; EOM and architecture. All proposals must be submitted through the conference's database at https://swpaca.org/app. For details on using the submission database and on the application process in general (including submitting proposals for roundtables and preformed panels), please see the FAQS & Resources tab on https://swpaca.org/. For information on how to submit a proposal for a multi-paper panel, please view the above FAQs & Resources link. The deadline for submissions is October 31, 2026. More details are here: https://swpaca.org/graduate-student-paper-awards/. SWPACA also offers travel fellowships for undergraduate and graduate students as well as contingent faculty: https://swpaca.org/travel-awards-students-faculty/. Registration and travel information for the conference is available at https://swpaca.org/albuquerque-conference/. In addition, please check out the organization's peer-reviewed, scholarly journal, Dialogue: The Interdisciplinary Journal of Popular Culture and Pedagogy, at https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/dialogue/. If you have any questions about the Esotericism, Occultism, and Magic area, please contact its Area Chair, Dr. George J. Sieg, Luna Community College, georgejsieg@gmail.com . If you have general questions about the conference, please contact us at support@swpaca.org, and a member of the executive team will get back to you. This will be a fully in-person conference. items.fullDescription: Nonfiction film and media have played a crucial role in advocating for animal welfare, rights and liberation. Although short videos and a number of documentaries were produced and distributed with activist purposes during the 1980s, it is during the so-called “documentary renaissance” of the early twenty-first century, together with the communicative advances of digital media, that nonfiction moving images emerged as a medium capable of reaching more mainstream audiences, becoming a central cultural tool for instigating transformative change in humans’ speciesist practices and attitudes toward nonhuman animals.

items.title: Watching Cinema Theoretically: Psychoanalytic Perspectives on Film
items.excerpt: The relation between a theory and its so-called “object” always poses the danger of reducing an art form (in this case film) to a mere instance testifying to the validity of the theory. In this way, the theory provides the “genus” of which a given film will be a mere “species”. The application of psychoanalytic ideas or Marxist concepts to film would ther...
items.fullDescription: The relation between a theory and its so-called “object” always poses the danger of reducing an art form (in this case film) to a mere instance testifying to the validity of the theory. In this way, the theory provides the “genus” of which a given film will be a mere “species”. The application of psychoanalytic ideas or Marxist concepts to film would therefore run the risk of depriving the specificity and singularity of the object in favour of the hegemony of the theory. Here, theory would truly live up to its theological vocation (the “theo” in theory refers to God) standing transcendentally above its “object” upon which it would cast its daunting shadow.

items.fullDescription: CFP: Red Reading the Modern Novel Society for Novel Studies (Vancouver, BC; 13-16 May 2027) The organizer seeks papers that apply Red Reading to twentieth- and twenty-first century novels. The literary canon has been expanded brilliantly in the last few decades, and literary critical approaches have shifted away from modes of corrosive critique. There remains however, a dearth of work grounded in Indigenous epistemologies and critical approaches. As an initial response to this gap, this panel seeks to test Red Reading's utility for studies of the novel. Red reading is one of the most exciting new literary critical methods to emerge in this century. First coined in 2010 Jill Carter the term "Red Reading" has been echoed in different frames by Daniel Heath Justice and James H. Cox, worked out in medieval contexts by Brenna Duperon, and consolidated in a 2018 issue of transmotion edited by Scott Andrews. Most simply, it entails bringing Indigenous approaches to bear on non-Indigenous texts, placing "native perspectives at the center of the discussion," asking new questions of the canon, and drawing non-Indigenous texts into Indigenous epistemological, ethical, and historical frameworks (Andrews ii). It goes beyond just adding Indigenous texts to existing studies and courses to advance a new way of reading that shifts the entire frame of reference. Importantly, Red Reading's early adopters have urged non-Indigenous scholars to use it, making it accessible to scholars of all identities. Potential prompts: • How can Indigenous modes of thinking about story and narrative change the critical reception of modern novels? • What would it look like to apply Indigenous epistemologies to canonical texts? • What can we learn about modern novels by taking a Red Reading approach? • How can Red Reading help us both decolonize the curriculum and advance the goals of reconciliation? • What are the stakes of taking a non-Western, Indigenous approach to reading modern novels? • Are the lessons of postcolonialism and decolonial studies applicable here? Or does red reading constitute something different? • Is the modern novel itself amenable to a Red Reading approach, or is it an ideological form that remains alien to Indigenous epistemologies? Queries and 250 word abstracts should be addressed to Stephen Ross at saross@uvic.ca. Deadline for receipt of abstracts is November 1, 2026.

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers: [Children's and Young Adult Literature] at CEA 2027 Apr. 1-3, 2027 | St. Louis, Missouri The Westin St. Louis Hotel https://cea-web.org/the-conference-hotel The College English Association, a gathering of scholar-teachers in English studies, welcomes proposals for presentations on Children's and Young Adult Literature for our 57th annual conference. Submit your proposal at www.cea-web.org Scholars and teachers of children's and YA lit intimately know the transformative power the right story at the right time can have on an elementary, middle, or high school student. We do not need reminding of how words, and how they are communicated, to young learners have the ability to grow cognitive processes and lead to future generations of lovers of the written word and future torchbearers of the significance of those words coming from the minds of human beings. Coalescing around the conference theme, we consider how the influence of diverse sculpted stories opens the door to deeper discernment across the curriculum. Conference Theme: Gateways For its 2027 annual conference, the College English Association (CEA) invites proposals for papers and panels that explore the theme of "Gateways" and their significance in literature, criticism, and pedagogy. Tracing its history back to French explorers in the second half of the 18th century, the great city of St. Louis began as a fur trading post named after King Louis IX of France and was established on the ancestral lands of the Osage Nation, Missouria, and Illini Confederacy. Becoming part of the United States through the Louisiana Purchase of 1803, the city famously came to be known as the "Gateway to the West," serving as a launching point for generations of explorers and settlers expanding the frontier. Yet, we must remember that the city also serves as a gateway to its past as part of indigenous lands transformed through its colonial history into a major river port and trading center that fostered migration both outwards and inwards for centuries. Today, St. Louis invites us to reflect on the continued significance of gateways in our 21st-century lives. GENERAL CALL FOR PAPERS GATEWAYS: For its 2027 annual conference, the College English Association (CEA) invites proposals for papers and panels that explore the theme of "Gateways" and their significance in literature, criticism, and pedagogy. Potential areas of interest: How do gateways expand literary and cultural spaces but also, as access points, mark out boundaries and limits? Do gateways invite gatekeepers to enable and limit access? Is it possible to imagine gateways without gatekeepers? How can we imagine literary and cultural gateways to foster inter-cultural, cross-cultural, and trans-cultural interactions? How do we envision pedagogical approaches to create gateways for our students to new literary vistas, critical thought, and professional opportunities? items.fullDescription: Childhood is far more than a stage of life - it is a dynamic social, cultural, historical and political construct that shapes individuals, communities and societies. The experiences, representations and rights of children influence not only personal development but also the future of education, healthcare, policy, culture and social justice. As contemporary societies grapple with rapid technological change, migration, inequality and evolving family structures, the study of childhood has become more relevant than ever. Over the past decades, Childhood Studies has emerged as a vibrant interdisciplinary field, challenging traditional assumptions about children and recognising them as active social actors with their own voices, agency and rights. Today, researchers and practitioners from across the humanities, social sciences, education, health, law and the arts are exploring childhood from diverse theoretical and methodological perspectives. This conference provides an international platform for scholars, researchers, practitioners, policymakers, educators, artists and professionals to discuss contemporary debates, emerging challenges and innovative research on children and childhood. We particularly welcome interdisciplinary approaches that bridge disciplines and offer fresh perspectives on children's lives in local and global contexts. We invite proposals on topics including, but not limited to: Childhood psychology and child development Anthropology of children and childhood Sociology of childhood Children, identity and belonging Children's agency and participation Children's rights and child advocacy Childhood, inequality and social justice Children, migration and displacement Childhood, conflict and humanitarian crises Childhood, disability and inclusion Early childhood education and care Formal, informal and non-formal education Children and digital technologies Children, social media and digital childhoods Children, media and media representations of childhood Contemporary children's culture Children's play, creativity and imagination Children, family and parenthood Childhood and wellbeing Children and mental health Childhood, memory and intergenerational relationships Historical perspectives on childhood Children and the law Ethics and methodologies of child-centred research Children's literature and literature about childhood Children and childhood in art, film and popular culture Environmental education and children's relationships with nature Global and comparative perspectives on childhood

Topics may include, but are not limited to: Arts & Humanities: AI in creativity, authorship, performance, and cultural identity. Business: Automation, labor ethics, and corporate responsibility. items.fullDescription: Conference Themes We invite submissions that engage with the ethics of artificial intelligence in both specific and general applications. Topics may include, but are not limited to: Arts & Humanities: AI in creativity, authorship, performance, and cultural identity. Business: Automation, labor ethics, and corporate responsibility. Education: AI in teaching, learning, and research integrity; utilizing AI for student success initiatives and learning accommodations; ethical applications and questions related to AI in scholarly activity; AI in K-12 education. Environmental Impact: AI and sustainability, climate modeling, and AI resource consumption. Healthcare & Medicine: Projection models for patient disease development; treatment individuation; individualized medicine; bias in treatment. Law & Policy: Privacy and data usage; the legitimacy of AI in government. Library & Information Science: AI and the new digital divide; algorithmic bias; AI accuracy, mis- and dis-information. Philosophy: AI as moral agents; AI's effect on human autonomy and decision making; human-AI interfaces and the locus of moral responsibility. Science: AI fabrication of scientific data or references; legitimacy of sources for AI training; drug discovery; intellectual property of data from AI discoveries. Theology: AI in moral theology and bioethics; AI applications in healthcare; theological responses to AI development, including those offered in light of Antiqua et nova (2025) and Magnifica Humanitas (2026). Social Justice & Equity: Accessibility, bias, and discrimination in AI systems. Social Sciences: AI as a research tool for data analysis and methodology; AI systems as social entities and their behavioral impacts; algorithmic bias in social research; AI's effects on human social structures and interactions. Proposal Submissions We welcome proposals for individual papers, panels, workshops, or creative presentations. Submission Guidelines Submissions should include: Proposed Title Abstract (250-300 words) clearly outlining the project and its ethical dimension(s). Disciplinary Alignment or Keywords (up to 5 keywords) that help to categorize your proposal. Format Preference (paper, panel, interactive discussion/workshop, or 7-minute lightning talk). Short Bio (100-300 words) for each presenter, including institutional affiliation. All submissions will undergo blind peer review by the interdisciplinary planning committee. Please submit the above information to the online submission form (https://form.jotform.com/262075169144054)

items.fullDescription: The erotic is a point of infinite signification, a navel in humanity’s symbolic circuit. However, despite its resistance to formalization, it is always in the process of not being written. As Octavio Paz insists, the erotic is a metaphor indelible to the human. As such, it is unsurprising that the manifestations of the erotic in subjective embodied experience are variable and correspond to equally plural treatments of it across the academic panorama. This diverse archive is bound by certain distinguishable threads, in terms of the potentiality of the erotic, its singular relation to language, and to the sphere of sexuality.

In 2024, sexually explicit AI-generated deepfakes of Taylor Swift circulated widely online, demonstrating a very different but related form of imag...
items.fullDescription: In January 2026, murals of faceless female silhouettes in yoga poses were scratched around the genital area in the Indian city of Gwalior. The figures depicted no identifiable women; they were attacked anyway. In 2024, sexually explicit AI-generated deepfakes of Taylor Swift circulated widely online, demonstrating a very different but related form of image violation. Across a scratched public wall and a fabricated digital image, the same question emerges: what happens when an image of a woman becomes the surface upon which sexualisation, humiliation or punishment is performed? This special issue asks where, if anywhere, a woman’s image can be assumed to be safe.

This international academic event seeks to bring together researchers, academics, artists, educators, and professionals from different disciplines to explore the historical, cultural, social, artistic, scientific, and technological dimensions of healing and well-being. The Congress proposes a dialogue between nineteenth-century traditions and contemporary approaches to health and healing, examining continuities, transformations, exchanges, and tensions across the Hispanic world, Asia, Latin America, and the Caribbean. Particular attention will be given to the ways in which literature, art, spirituality, traditional medicine, bodily practices, digital technologies, and community experiences have shaped understandings and practices of healing. Suggested themes include: Genealogies of Healing in Nineteenth-Century Hispanic Culture Representations of Illness in Nineteenth-Century Literature and the Press Art and Healing: Music, Dance, Painting, and Theatre as Therapeutic Practices Dialogues between Allopathic Medicine and Traditional Healing Systems Spirituality, Religion, and Healing Practices Healing through Words: Narratives, Discourse, and Therapeutic Processes Convergences between Bodily Practices (Yoga, Pranayama, Sports) and Holistic Health Healing Traditions in Asia and the Caribbean: Exchanges with the Hispanic World Digital Health, Applications, Platforms, and Well-Being Monitoring Ethical and Clinical Risks of Chatbots and Mental Health Technologies Social Media, Virality, and Their Impact on Emotional Health Attention, Cognition, and Technology Digital Churches, the Spiritual Economy, and New Forms of Religiosity Education and Well-Being Public Health Policies in Digital and Multicultural Environments Interdisciplinarity in Health: Intersections between Art, Science, and Technology Imaginaries of Good and Evil in Processes of Illness and Healing Community Well-Being and Territorial Experiences Researchers interested in participating are invited to submit proposals in accordance with the Congress guidelines.
