items.fullDescription: Heidelberg Center for American Studies Annual Interdisciplinary Spring Academy Conference Heidelberg, Germany, April 5-9, 2027 Call for Papers The Heidelberg Center for American Studies (HCA) invites applications for its annual Spring Academy on American Culture, Economics, Geography, History, Literature, Politics, and Religion to be held from April 5-9, 2027. The HCA Spring Academy provides 20 international Ph.D. students with the opportunity to present and thoroughly discuss their ongoing Ph.D. projects. The conference offers a forum for Ph.D. candidates in which they can present their research candidly and receive valuable feedback. We encourage applications that range broadly across the arts, humanities, and social sciences and pursue an interdisciplinary approach. Participants can present thesis projects on any subject relating to the study of the United States of America. Possible topics include American identity, issues of ethnicity, gender, transatlantic relations, U.S. domestic and foreign policy, economics, and various aspects of American religion, geography, history, literature, law, musicology, and culture. We also welcome proposals focused on the North American continent at large, i.e. Canada, Central America, and the Caribbean. Participants are requested to prepare a 20-minute presentation of their research project, which will be followed by a 40-minute discussion. The Spring Academy aims to create a congenial atmosphere for scholarly exchange in order to inspire future collaborations and foster networking opportunities for participants. The Heidelberg Center for American Studies is prepared to provide accommodation during the conference week. Thanks to a small travel fund, the Spring Academy can subsidize travel expenses for participants registered and residing in developing and soft-currency countries. Applicants for the travel fund must document the necessity for financial aid and explain how they plan to cover any potentially remaining expenses. Additionally, a letter of recommendation from their doctoral advisor is required. items.fullDescription: CFP: Queer Mediterranean - Sex, Gender, and Social Change April 1-3, 2027, Smith College (Northampton, MA) Queer Mediterranean: Sex, Gender, and Social Change is a conference that brings together scholars, artists, and thinkers to explore queer cultures across the Mediterranean from a transhistorical and transnational perspective, with particular attention to the experiences, voices, and cultural productions of women. The conference aims to explore how queer subjects have navigated, resisted, or reimagined structures of power and belonging across the Mediterranean. What does it mean to think the Mediterranean queerly? What new frameworks, methods, or archives emerge from this approach? While centering women's experiences, we remain fully open to contributions that explore queer life in all its forms. Queer Mediterranean explores what becomes visible when we shift the center of queer theory away from Anglophone frameworks. How do Mediterranean histories complicate dominant narratives of queer identity and liberation? How do Mediterranean perspectives challenge or expand existing models of queer community, kinship, and belonging? What do transnational approaches to queerness reveal about the relationship between queerness, language, and translation? The conference will take place April 1-3, 2027 at Smith College. Hotel accommodations will be provided for all accepted panelists. --- We invite proposals for papers that highlight the richness and diversity of queer experiences across time and place. We welcome scholarly work from across the humanities, social sciences, and arts and are particularly interested in interdisciplinary and transnational perspectives. Topics might include (but are not limited to): Queer histories, archives and memory Queer kinship, family, and belonging Queer migration and diaspora Language, translation, and queer expression Queer literature, film, and visual cultures Queer bodies & embodiment Queer geographies and spaces Queer ecologies and the more-than-human Mediterranean Queer labor and economies Queer tourism and Mediterranean imaginaries Colonialism, postcolonialism, and queerness Queer art and creative practice as resistance Queer temporality and futurity Teaching the queer Mediterranean Abstracts (250-300 words) should be sent through the following google form by November 15, 2026. We will notify accepted panelists by December 15, 2026. Contact: Adrián Gras-Velázquez (agrasvelazquez@smith.edu) Gianna Albaum (galbaum@smith.edu)

items.fullDescription: In the 2000s and 2010s, social networking facilitated citizen-based activism of enormous significance like #BlackLivesMatter and #MeToo. But in the 2020s, corporate enshittification and government surveillance have restricted the reach of social networking tools. For example, Elon Musk’s purchase of Twitter meant that many users left X rather than adapt their activist practices to the restrictive corporate environment (Tenbarge & Collier 2024). Instances such as the Trump administration’s use of social media posts to target international students during the Gaza protests caused many users to avoid social media altogether (Lonas Cochran 2025).

items.fullDescription: CFP: 28th Southeast Conference for Languages, Literatures, and Film (Feb 27-28, 2027) in St. Petersburg, Florida (on the University of South Florida St. Petersburg Campus) Languages and Cultures in a Changing World: Identity, Responsibility, and Justice Abstracts for papers (and panels) are now being considered. Deadline for abstracts: Nov. 16, 2026 Selected papers will be published in a post-conference anthology. To view prior publication, visit the conference website. The SCFLLF welcomes papers on all aspects of literature, theoretical and applied linguistics, culture, philosophy, cultural history, film, other popular media, second language acquisition, and language pedagogy pertaining to non-English languages (ancient and modern). We would like to encourage (but not limit) submissions addressing our conference theme: Identity, Responsibility and Justice, in its broadest understanding. Selected papers will be published in a post-conference anthology. The humanities and the study of languages are facing changing institutional and social expectations. These changes encourage us to reconsider what work we do and the people and communities our work serves. To whom and to what, are artists, scholars and teachers accountable? How do languages, literatures, films, and other forms of cultural expression preserve or challenge established narratives and structures? How do they engage with different identities? How can they help us understand the present and/or imagine different futures? What responsibilities come with teaching and learning languages as well as with studying, interpreting, and representing other cultures? This conference invites scholars working in non-English languages, literatures, film and media, cultural studies, applied and theoretical linguistics, second-language acquisition, and language pedagogy to explore these and related questions from a wide range of disciplinary, theoretical, historical, and methodological perspectives. The conference theme, Identity, Responsibility, and Justice, is deliberately broad. Responsibility may involve our relationships with students and communities, with texts and their histories, with linguistic and cultural traditions, or with the institutions in which we teach and conduct research. Or responsibility can be interrogated with regard to artists and art, in a broad sense. Justice can also be approached in diverse ways. It may involve social justice, questions of representation and recognition, historical memory, inclusion and exclusion, or access and lack thereof to language learning. Justice may also concern translation and cultural mediation or the ways in which literature, film, language, and other cultural practices engage with conflict, inequality, trauma, discrimination, displacement, and/or social change. The SCFLLF keynote speaker is Adam Schwartz (Associate Professor of Language, Culture & Society, Oregon State University). Dr. Schwartz's research addresses Spanish language education and Spanish-English multilingualisms in the U.S. He takes particular interest in intersections of language, race and racism, wherein questions of identity, responsibility and justice persist. In addition to various articles and chapters, he has authored three books. These include Spanish So White: Conversations on the Inconvenient Racism of a 'Foreign' Language Education (2023). He is also the co-author of Aquí se habla: Centering the Local and Personal in Spanish Language Education (2025) as well as Language, Identity and Justice: The Anthropolitical Worlds of Ana Celia Zentella (2026). Some suggestions of topics and their artistic representations include: identity, responsibility, and justice represented in literature, art, film, and other forms of popular media, including social media influence of film and literature on the public and private sphere reassessing the purpose and value of language teaching expressions and perceptions of trauma in response to injustice justice in utopian fictional worlds addressing and expressing identity in the language classroom questions of identity in literature, film, the arts, and other popular media responsibility issues in production and reception of artistic expressions responsibilities associated with researching and representing cultures apart or in comparison to our own the broader influence of imaginary worlds created in film, literature, the visual arts, and other forms of media on real political and personal justice language and linguistic-related topics concerning identity, responsibility, and justice other topics Please submit a proposal (of no more than 250 words) for a single paper or a full panel (max. of 3 presentations) on the conference webpage. We can only accept online submissions. Please contact Margit Grieb (grieber@usf.edu) if you have any questions.

items.fullDescription: When, in September 2026, a post declaring the actress Katrina Kaif "finished" following her return to public life after childbirth accumulated lakhs of views and comments, the disproportion between judgement and object became, itself, the more legible text. A comparable structure recurred that same year for the South Korean singer Jennie, whose performances at Mad Cool Festival and Lollapalooza Chicago drew, alongside widespread acclaim, a coordinated wave of "netizen" commentary deriding her "leaner frame" — two women, two national contexts, two entirely unrelated bodily "failures" (one insufficiently youthful, the other insufficiently substantial), and yet an identical infrastructure of mass, public, collectively affirmed judgement.

items.title: Destination Management and Mobility Justice for Sustainable Human and More-than-human Futures: Approaching Florence (and Destinations Beyond) in Motio
items.excerpt: In this interdisciplinary conference, we seek to examine critical issues in the field of global Destination Management and Tourism Mobilities in pursuit of means, modes and practices to promote a greater Mobility Justice within, between, and beyond destinations (Sheller 2018; 2024). Situated within the Florentine context, this conference offers fertile gr...
items.fullDescription: In this interdisciplinary conference, we seek to examine critical issues in the field of global Destination Management and Tourism Mobilities in pursuit of means, modes and practices to promote a greater Mobility Justice within, between, and beyond destinations (Sheller 2018; 2024). Situated within the Florentine context, this conference offers fertile ground for cross-pollination between Florence and other destinations concerned with how Destination Managers and Destination Management Organizations (DMOs) can be pivotal actors, agencies, and organizations committed to a more just, sustainable, and responsible mobile world. As the politics of mobility play out in real time through the bodies and streets, we see local, national and transnational governance struggle to keep pace with the impacts and drivers of climate change, urbanization, and migration. All the while we watch as mass tourism and overtourism thread impacts through micro, meso, and macro scales. Simultaneously, migrants, refugees, asylum seekers, undocumented, stateless, and trafficked persons experience increasing pressures and injustices through the same forces that support the most mobility privileged in global tourist flows. In this entangled web of mobility regimes and infrastructures, it is important to examine where travel and tourism have historically been a cultural force for promoting peace and dialogue, as much as examining where conflict, friction, and tensions have arisen from them. Destinations offer an opportunity to analyze and intervene at specific sites of human migrations and mobilities, and what in hopes of more just tourism mobilities in destinations across the world. Florence is no stranger to conflicts over tourism mobilities and tensions within its unique identity as a site of global patrimony. As a destination caught in the crosshairs of its rich past and an uncertain future in this age of polycrisis, conflicting representations and identities intersect, diverge, and weave a complex social fabric. Destination Management offers a targeted lens through which to interrogate the relation between global travel, tourism and mobility justice in Florence and beyond. As a UNESCO World Heritage Site, Florence represents a rich cultural tourism destination that is increasingly impacted by increasingly global flows and circulations of people, objects, artifacts, information, resources and capital. It has resulted in intersecting crises of housing displacement and homelessness, food insecurity, growing civil protest, increasing environmental resource and climatic constraints, uneven distribution of tourist fluxes between major and minor cultural sites, and loss of local goodwill in response to the immobilities created by tourism. This conference seeks to bring to light the complexities of questions of justice in a hypermobile world. How does one respect cultural heritage while local peoples and cultures suffer across so many dimensions, often deprived of their cultural rights, unable to access their own heritage sites? How do we support human and more-than-human futures, adaptable and responsive to environmental constraints, changes, and challenges? Many questions arise that require interdisciplinary perspectives. We invite papers to contribute to the emerging field of Destination Management, focusing on the intersections of issues in social, cultural, environmental, and mobility justice within the roles and responsibilities of Destination Managers and DMOs (Destination Management Organizations). We welcome a wide range of disciplinary perspectives and methods, including case study analyses, historical or contemporary mobilities, and theoretical contributions that are committed to exploring what Justice means within Destination Management theory and practice. Thematically, we ask contributors to examine how questions of justice can be integrated into interdisciplinary Destination Management scholarship that contend with the domains of travel and tourism. Submissions can include both normative and empirical research broadly relevant to informing questions of Justice and Mobilities, and can broadly range from social sciences, STEM, humanities, and arts fields, and present either contemporary or historical perspectives. We aim to explore where various areas of justice can be connected to the objectives of Destination Management research as a growing interdisciplinary field. We encourage scholars and practitioners to investigate the applicability of distributive, deliberative, procedural, restorative, and epistemic justice in the framework of their presented contributions. We are interested in case studies which either (A) center their analyses on Florence, Italy (or the region of Tuscany) in order to seek translatable and transversal solutions for other destinations, or (B) center on global destinations beyond that bring critical insight into the issues facing Florence. We are seeking to find "common ground" amongst the examined problem spaces that exist across destinations to build a growing literature concerned with promoting Mobility Justice within Destination Management. Theoretical contributions should include insight or practical application to transversal issues across Florence and other destinations. SUBMISSION GUIDELINES: We ask for 300-word abstracts, submitted with a separate cover page that includes title, name, affiliation, and a short bio of the author(s) of a maximum of 300 words, which can be submitted to dstm@gonzaga.edu by November 25th, 2026. The conference will be held from March 11th to 12th at Gonzaga in Florence, a school of Gonzaga University based in the historic center of the city of Florence. It will be open to the public, by registration. There will be no registration fee to attend the conference. As our inaugural conference, we are unable to offer travel funds at this time. Topical Areas: 1. Mobility Justice (motility, capabilities approach, migration, transport, space, accessibility, flows) a. Migration, refugees, stateless persons, human trafficking and modern day slavery b. Critical Disability Studies & mobility infrastructures for travel & tourism industries c. The Right to the City, labour, and yransportation equity d. Mobility, technological transformation, and electrification e. Climate Mobility Justice and immigration/refugee crises 2. Social Justice (intersectionality, human rights, kinopolitics distributive justice, reparation, processual justice) a. Indigenous Rights and Land Consent b. Human rights Abuses in the travel and tourism industry c. Intercultural exchange for responsible, sustainable, and peace tourism d. Reparative justice, public policy, media, and communications e. Critical Disability Studies and transport justice 3. Cultural Justice: (heritage studies, restoration and repatriation, cultural property, political ecology) a. Art, antiquities, museum studies, and decolonization b. Cultural heritage, human rights, and access to culture c. Cultural property trafficking, return and restitution, reclamation, and reparations d. Museum security, contemporary eco-vandalism and protest movements e. Conflicts in historiography of heritage and Post-conflict reconstruction 4. Environmental Justice (environmental racism, geoengineering, pollution and carbon, biodiversity and reparations, More-than-human ethics): a. National parks, seascapes, urban green space, and depavement movements b. Plastic pollution, chemical colonialism, exposomics, and water protectors c. Protected habitats, ecotourism and politics of spared or shared land d. Agriculture, food Justice, "The Commons", land sovereignty, and eco-activism e. Botanical gardens, zoos, "beasts of burden", and more-than-human mobility Conference Organizers: Denise Regina Percequillo Hossom Gonzaga University Alesia Koush Gonzaga University UNESCO Chair - University of Siena

items.fullDescription: At many universities, learning communities foster connectedness and belonging among students. Learning communities are typically composed of cohorts of students taking aligned first-year classes, but they take many other forms as well. At their best, they promote the perspective that learning is a collective activity in which knowledge is constructed through relationships with peers, professors, and communities, bringing together diverse voices and interdisciplinary perspectives. items.excerpt: We invite proposals for papers from scholars of literature, theology, and philosophy to explore the intersection of St. Thomas Aquinas' thought and the dramatic works of William Shakespeare. The age of Shakespeare was steeped in and shaped by the intellectual contributions of Aquinas (informed by Aristotle), but little critical attention has been paid to...
items.fullDescription: We invite proposals for papers from scholars of literature, theology, and philosophy to explore the intersection of St. Thomas Aquinas' thought and the dramatic works of William Shakespeare. The age of Shakespeare was steeped in and shaped by the intellectual contributions of Aquinas (informed by Aristotle), but little critical attention has been paid to the connections between the Angelic Doctor and the Bard. We seek to bring their works into rich and sustained dialogue with one another, so as to inspire a fresh critical engagement with both thinkers. To complement our keynote address by Hannibal Hamlin (The Ohio State University), we welcome papers that use Aquinas as an interpretive lens for Shakespearean drama; draw on Shakespeare to illustrate or complicate Aquinas' understanding of human and divine realities; address the broader historical, theological, and philosophical contexts linking the two figures (including their shared reception of Aristotle). Topics may include, but are not limited to: An analysis of a particular virtue or vice, as understood by Aquinas, found on the Shakespearean stage. The dramatization of other elements of Thomistic anthropology. Aquinas and Shakespeare's respective receptions of Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics . The approach Aquinas and Shakespeare each takes toward Scripture. Other theological themes in the works of Shakespeare and Aquinas, such as divine providence and free will; temptation and sin; grace, conversion, redemption, and salvation; natural law and positive law. The organizers intend to publish an edited volume on this subject with a university press. Following the conference, select presenters will be invited to submit full chapters for consideration. The organizers intend to publish an edited volume on this subject with a univerity press. Following the conference, select presenters will be invited to submit full chapters for consideration. Proposals for 20-minute papers should include a paper title, 3-5 keywords, a 300-word abstract, and a short bio-bibliographical note , and be sent via email to all three of the following by November 30, 2026: Sr. Maria Frassati Jakupcak, OP (maria.jakupcak@stthom.edu) Fr. Jordan Zajac, OP (jzajac@providence.edu) Sr. Mary Edith Humphries, OP (srmedith@aquinascollege.edu). Decisions will be communicated by December 14, 2026 . There is no conference registration fee.

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers: Literary Gardens: Cultivation, Movement, and Modernism An International Online Conference | February 12-13, 2027 | Online sponsored by The Elizabeth von Arnim Society in conversation with The Literary Garden: The Cultivation of Plants & Gardens in Narratives Stephen and Peter Sachs Museum, Missouri Botanical Garden The Elizabeth von Arnim Society invites paper proposals for an international online conference on literary gardens, held in conversation with the Missouri Botanical Garden exhibit The Literary Garden: The Cultivation of Plants & Gardens in Narratives (Sachs Museum, May 2026-March 2027), curated by Nezka Pfeifer. Inspired by the exhibition's wide-ranging exploration of plants and gardens, this conference will consider gardens as spaces of literary cultivation, movement, and modernity. Gardens are never simply settings: they are imagined spaces, sites of labor and care, refuge and restoration, social and cultural exchange, but also places of exclusion, transgression, and imperialist pilfering. Plants, people, texts, ideas, and botanical knowledge move through them. Gardens can therefore illuminate modernism's preoccupation with mobility, displacement, belonging, transformation, and the relationship between the human and more-than-human worlds. The conference centers on modernism, broadly conceived, including fin-de-siècle precursors and modernism's later extensions and legacies. We are particularly interested in women's garden writing, including that of Elizabeth von Arnim, as well as the ways gardens participate in transnational literary and cultural networks. We welcome work on African American, Caribbean, diasporic, queer, Indigenous, and other perspectives that complicate and expand histories of modernism and the literary garden. We warmly encourage you to share this call with colleagues, graduate students, and independent scholars Keynote Speakers: Nezka Pfiefer, curator of The Literary Garden: The Cultivation of Plants & items.fullDescription: Overview | South Mediterranean University, Tunisia Hybrid Format: In-person and Online Participation The SMU Conference on AI-Era Teaching: Innovative Pedagogy and Reimagined Classrooms will take place at South Mediterranean University, Tunisia. This research oriented event brings together scholars, educators, instructional designers, and researchers to explore evidence-based pedagogical innovation in technology-mediated and AI-enhanced learning environments. This conference provides an international platform to present academic research, foster interdisciplinary dialogue, and advance collaboration on the future of teaching and learning in the AI era. The 2027 SMU Conference, themed "AI-Era Teaching: Innovative Pedagogy and Reimagined Classrooms," examines how AI and emerging educational technologies reshape instructional design, classroom engagement, assessment, and learning ecosystems. Key focus areas include measurable learning outcomes, ethical and inclusive AI integration, pedagogical quality assurance, and student competency development in hybrid and digital environments. We invite researchers, practitioners, instructional designers, and graduate students worldwide to submit original research, empirical studies, and case studies on innovative pedagogy, AI-enhanced instruction, learning analytics, engagement strategies, and inclusive practices.

items.fullDescription: Living with the Wild: Wildlife, Civilization, and the Trouble of Coexistence University of Catania, 1-3 March 2027 Abstract deadline: 30 November 2026 The final conference of the WILD-CONNECT project, Wildlife Circulation and the Enactment of Civilization in Diachronic Perspective, invites contributions exploring how relations between the "wild" and the "civilized" have been shaped across historical, political, and cultural contexts. The conference approaches these categories as historically produced and mutually constitutive, and examines how their boundaries are continually renegotiated through institutions, practices, imaginaries, and material forms of life. We welcome contributions from anthropology, history, political ecology, environmental humanities, and related fields addressing wildlife circulation, control, transformation, and reintroduction, as well as the interconnected processes of dewilding and rewilding. Possible topics include domestication, conservation and ecological restoration; colonial and postcolonial wildlife governance; sovereignty, borders and wildlife circulation; everyday encounters with wildlife; scientific, legal and economic classifications of living beings; and the unintended consequences and limits of wildlife governance. The conference will feature keynote contributions by Vanessa Manceron (CNRS), Marcy Norton (University of Pennsylvania), and Erik Gómez-Baggethun (Norwegian University of Life Sciences). Accepted papers will be circulated among participants in advance, and contributions presented at the conference will be considered for inclusion in a collective volume or a special issue of an international journal in environmental humanities. Living_with_the_Wild_Call Please submit: an abstract of 300-400 words; a short biographical note of 100-150 words; institutional affiliation, if any, and contact details. Submissions should be sent to mara.benadusi@unict.it and lorenzo.coccoli@unict.it. Deadline : 30 November 2026 Notification of acceptance : 2 January 2027

items.fullDescription: 2027 marks the 50th anniversary of the film now generally known as Episode IV: A New Hope , the first instalment in the hugely successful Star Wars franchise created by George Lucas. As beloved as it is divisive, Star Wars now straddles multiple decades and generations while proliferating across narrative media (novels, comics, games, animation, TV). It provides a series of compelling case studies in the relationship between creativity and commerce, from the foundation of Lucasfilm during the New Hollywood period to the 21st century Disney-era, and it has developed via a complex interplay between cutting-edge technological innovation, nostalgia, and mythmaking.

items.fullDescription: Over the past three decades, fan studies have developed sophisticated accounts of participatory culture, collective intelligence, affective engagement, and transformative practices (Jenkins 2006; Booth 2015; Hills 2017). At the same time, scholarship has increasingly addressed the investigative dimensions of audience participation. Mittell’s concept of “forensic fandom” (2009), for example, highlights practices of close reading, clue collection, speculation, and collaborative interpretation in response to complex narrative worlds. Fans thus become active investigators who uncover hidden meanings, solve mysteries, and assemble fragmented information across media texts. More recently, such investigative practices have expanded beyond fictional worlds.

items.fullDescription: Myths have long shaped how humans understand and interact with the natural world. This edited collection examines how contemporary science fiction streaming television draws on mythology to explore humanity's relationship with the environment. Through the lens of ecocriticism, this collection will analyze how narratives represent, question, and critique environmental responsibility, ecological interconnectedness, and humanity's impact on Earth, or other worlds. Since 2008, John Perlich and David Whitt have co-edited three books on comparative mythology: Sith, Slayers, Stargates, and Cyborgs (2008), Millennial Mythmaking (2010), and Myth in the Modern World(2014). This fourth collection, which will be published by McFarland & Company, seeks to bring together scholars and cultural critics from a variety of fields (e.g., mythology, environmental studies, media, cultural studies, literature, political science, anthropology, sociology, communication studies) to examine contemporary and original science fiction television on streaming services. Streaming platforms have emerged as premier destinations for ambitious, avant-garde, commercially successful, and critically acclaimed science fiction. The following is a partial list of original science fiction shows on various streaming platforms: · Amazon Prime Video: Fallout, The Expanse, The Rig, Outer Range · Apple TV+: Foundation, Silo, For All Mankind, Pluribus, Monarch: Legacy of Monsters, Dark Matter, Star City, Invasion · Disney+: Star Wars (The Mandalorian, Andor, Ahsoka, Visions, Skeleton Crew), Marvel (Loki, Moon Knight) · HBO Max: The Last of Us, Dune: Prophecy, Raised by Wolves, Station Eleven · Hulu: Paradise, Solar Opposites · Netflix: Stranger Things, Black Mirror, Love, Death + Robots, 3 Body Problem, Sweet Tooth, Dark, The Eternaut, The Rain, The Silent Sea · Peacock: The Ark, Twisted Metal · Paramount+: Halo, Star Trek (Discovery, Lower Decks, Picard, Starfleet Academy, Strange New Worlds) The rich and varied programming on these streaming services provides a myriad of opportunities to examine contemporary science fiction television in terms of mythology and the environment. Some potential topics include: · Creation myths and the making of new worlds and ecosystems · The Hero's Journey and the environment · The impact of science and technology on the environment · Monsters, aliens and others environmental threats · Climate change, apocalyptic and dystopian worlds · Ecofeminism and mythology · Environmental activism · Allusions to mythic protectors (e.g., Gaia, Artemis, Demeter, Nüwa, Sedna, etc.) Please submit a proposal by December 1, 2026. Proposals should include: - a 500-1000 word abstract - brief author bio - contact information Chapters will be limited to 5000-6000 words and must follow APA style guidelines (7th edition). Send questions and proposals to both co-editors. John Perlich Bemidji State University john.perlich@bemidjistate.edu David Whitt Nebraska Wesleyan University dfw@nebrwesleyan.edu

items.title: The Four Horsemen of the Bropocalypse: Power and Culture Under a Tech Oligarchy
items.location: Bloomington, Indiana, United States · Indiana University
items.excerpt: CALL FOR PROPOSALS The Four Horsemen of the Bropocalypse: Power and Culture Under a Tech Oligarchy March 25-27, Bloomington, IN, Indiana University Bloomington The first quarter of the twenty-first century has been organized, to a degree that bears sustained scholarly attention, by a small cohort of men whose private fortunes rival the budgets of nation-s...
items.fullDescription: CALL FOR PROPOSALS The Four Horsemen of the Bropocalypse: Power and Culture Under a Tech Oligarchy March 25-27, Bloomington, IN, Indiana University Bloomington The first quarter of the twenty-first century has been organized, to a degree that bears sustained scholarly attention, by a small cohort of men whose private fortunes rival the budgets of nation-states, whose platforms mediate the social and epistemic lives of billions, and whose biographical idiosyncrasies have become structural features of global infrastructure. Steve Jobs furnished the template; Mark Zuckerberg, Jeff Bezos, Elon Musk, and Peter Thiel have inherited and transformed it. This conference takes the tech founder seriously as a political, economic, aesthetic, and theological problem, and as an object adequate to humanistic inquiry. The planning committee invites proposals for individual papers, pre-constituted panels, and roundtables across three streams - the Horsemen, their Mounts, their Kingdom. Comparative, transnational, and historically minded approaches are particularly welcome. Stream One: The Horsemen The Four Leaders of the Bropocalypse The figures themselves - as biographies, personae, cultural texts, and authors and products of their own myths. Questions to consider: How do we read the founder's letter, the keynote, the congressional testimony, the tweet? What work does biography do for the founder, and the founder for biography? How are their bodies stylized, optimized, and displayed? What is the cultural work of the turtleneck, the gilet, the cage match, the longevity protocol, the pronatalist announcement? How do spatial fantasies, such as the bunker, the compound, the rocket, the company town, relate to longer traditions of utopia, sovereignty, and flight? Where do the horsemen sit in longer histories of capital - Hearst, Ford, Hughes, Rockefeller - and alongside transnational counterparts? Stream Two: The Mounts Technological Foundations of the Bropocalypse The material, infrastructural, and epistemic conditions that made these figures possible and that they have, in turn, reshaped - the technologies the horsemen ride. Work drawing on media theory, STS, infrastructure studies, and the political economy of computing is especially welcome. Questions to consider: How do recommender systems and engagement metrics constitute attention as a political resource? How should we read the fulfillment center, the algorithmically managed workplace, the gig contract? What happens to the worker when the workplace is built to render the worker illegible? What are the climatic, hydrological, and territorial costs of the immaterial satellite constellations, undersea cables, data centers? What models of mind, language, and sociality are inscribed in the chatbot, the agent, the avatar? How do these systems reshape pedagogy, friendship, intimacy, grief, work? Stream Three: The Kingdom Institutional Context of the Bropocalypse The regulatory, financial, philanthropic, cultural, and political ecology that has enabled, legitimated, and at moments resisted the formation under analysis - the terrain across which the horsemen ride. Questions to consider: What is the worldview of contemporary venture capital, and how is it produced and reproduced through the manifesto, the LP letter, the founder-mode essay? How has the research university - its endowments, donors, dropout mythologies - both produced and been remade by the founders it educated and abandoned? What does it mean that the largest funders of causes such as global health, climate response, and basic research are now the personal foundations of living billionaires? How should we understand the migration of significant fractions of tech capital toward the American right, and the ideological projects - network state, accelerationism, neoreaction - that have traveled with it? What can scholarship learn from counter-formations such as Wikipedia, the Fediverse, platform cooperativism, the union drive, and open protocol? Submission Guidelines Proposals for individual papers (20 minutes) should consist of an abstract of no more than 350 words and a brief bio (100 words). Panel and roundtable proposals should include a 250-word rationale alongside individual abstracts. Please indicate the stream; the committee reserves the right to reassign. Submissions at https://forms.gle/uf5jwkNVWDBHbVcq9 by December 1, 2026. Decisions by January 30, 2027. Please direct any questions to bropocalypse2027@gmail.com. Edward Dallis-Comentale, Erin Kelley, Amber Bowes, Robert Metaxatos Indiana University Bloomington

items.title: Globally Contested Imaginaries: Power and Tensions in the AI Era
items.excerpt: Globally Contested Imaginaries: Power and Tensions in the AI Era April 8-9th 2027 at the Annenberg School for Communication at the University of Pennsylvania Organized by the Center on Digital Culture and Society AND the Center for Advanced Research in Global Communication at the University of Pennsylvania AI does not enter the world as a stable technolog...
items.fullDescription: Globally Contested Imaginaries: Power and Tensions in the AI Era April 8-9th 2027 at the Annenberg School for Communication at the University of Pennsylvania Organized by the Center on Digital Culture and Society AND the Center for Advanced Research in Global Communication at the University of Pennsylvania AI does not enter the world as a stable technology with a single meaning. It is narrated, simultaneously and contradictorily, as inevitable progress, geopolitical threat, overhyped fad, development solution, environmental danger, creative partner, engine of extraction, force of displacement, or instrument of sovereignty. Its invocation reflects cultural specificity and global variance. Yet AI imaginaries, advanced by powerful actors with unequal yet unfixed power across the globe, aim to define what AI is and will become. However these projections do not travel unchanged or unchallenged; they are contested, appropriated, refused, and reconfigured across different geopolitical, cultural, linguistic, and material worlds. This symposium begins from the premise that AI's global significance is neither self-evident nor uniform. We approach AI as a global digital communication project that interrogates how technologies circulate and how their meanings are (re)assembled and contested as they move across different cultural and global contexts. We aim to address the slipperiness of AI: How does the moral valence of AI shift depending on the answers and tasks demanded of it across various contexts? What is gained and lost when AI is treated as a coherent entity rather than a contested terrain? Where do dominant and alternative AI imaginaries collide most visibly-and what do those collisions reveal about power, culture, human agency, labor, development, modernity and possibility in our present moment? We invite submissions that examine the worlds in which AI becomes imaginable and contestable: the differing global narratives, infrastructures, histories, and communicative practices that make it appear necessary, desirable, dangerous, or inevitable, as well as the counternarratives, movements, and alternative imaginaries that challenge such claims and propose other futures. In this symposium, we seek a range of scholarship that takes the asymmetries of power seriously and explores and challenges which visions of AI get amplified, resourced, and institutionalized-without treating those asymmetries as settled outcomes. We invite submissions from scholars working on the intricacies of AI's entanglements with one of the four panel subthemes below and are particularly open to receiving projects that reflect on the cultural specificity and global variances of these subthemes. Panels: Myths and Narratives Writing on the grand promises that encircle new technologies, Vincent Mosco contends, "Myths are not true or false, but living or dead." In line with this provocation, this panel invites papers that explore the various myths and narratives that animate AI imaginaries-past, present, and future. ? How do people imagine AI in ways that are particular to their local geopolitical context? ? How do race, ethnicity, class, and geography affect how AI narratives cohere and how far they travel? ? How might values-political, religious, or otherwise-inform how people conceptualize the purpose of AI? ? What types of hopes and fears are projected upon AI? What role do institutions play in the formation (and challenging) of AI narratives? ? What is the historical context or ideology at play with words like "AGI" or "superintelligence"? Labor Following the iPhone across its life cycle, Qiu, Gregg, and Crawford (2014) contend that the labor of making, designing, using, and managing digital technologies form one connected circuit, not separate worlds, of work. In the spirit of their theory of the "circuits of labour," this panel invites submissions that investigate the unequal, extractive, and interdependent labor practices and conditions of the AI era. ? How does AI interface with existing labor practices and hierarchies? ? How do workers themselves understand their relationship to AI: as displacement, augmentation, exploitation, or opportunity? How do they respond? ? How are certain forms of work sustaining AI's apparent autonomy (e.g., content moderation, data annotation, model training) narrated-or erased-in dominant accounts? How is their role being reasserted from below? ? What forms of infrastructural labor are marshaled for the growth of AI systems? In what ways is this relationship economically, socially, and environmentally relevant? ? How does the global division of AI labor map onto, reproduce, or unsettle older (asymmetric) economic geographies and relations? ? What happens to professional identity and expertise when AI is positioned as "superintelligence" or as a creative and intellectual "partner"? ? What light might earlier eras of automation or displacement anxiety (e.g., industrialization, computerization, offshoring) shed on our present moment? Resistance In this panel, we seek to understand resistance through Adorno's conceptualization of negative dialectics, wherein resistance functions neither by proposing a new, 'positive' alternative or by retreating to a naive notion of 'authentic' human nature. Rather, it operates precisely through contradiction as a critical force. We invite work that examines resistance to AI as a contradictory field, where forms of refusal, critique, and opposition reveal the limits of totalizing discourses, operate through the very systems they contest, and remain unsettled by the absence of a conclusive alternative. Submissions that address and expand on the following topics are welcome: ? How do practices of resistance challenge the exclusions, assumptions, and forms of domination in totalizing accounts of AI technological progress that seek to naturalize computational forms of classification, prediction, and control? ? How do forms of resistance to AI that expose the contradictions of totalizing technological discourses confront their own implication within these systems? In other words: How do forms of resistance to AI negotiate the contradiction of opposing AI systems, when the infrastructures, categories, and practices that enable critique may themselves be shaped by technological rationality? ? What does resistance to AI in various regions of the Global Majority at the present conjuncture reveal about the contradictions of global capitalism and how histories of colonialism continue to shape contemporary struggles over technology, sovereignty, and competing visions of modernity? Social Life This panel explores social life as another contested terrain of AI's reach and impact. We invite papers that address how global communities merge their nuanced adoption and relationship to AI with the habits, relationships, and expectations of everyday life. ? How does AI become ordinary through practices of scrolling, posting, sharing, and messaging? When is its presence noticed, questioned, or taken for granted? ? How do memes and everyday conversations make AI appear useful, threatening, intimate, or irrelevant across different cultural worlds? ? How do pleasure, pain, desire, and other embodied experiences exceed the categories through which platforms make people knowable? ? How do people negotiate intimacy, care, and belonging through media platforms and what happens to expectations of trust and reciprocity when an interlocutor may not be human? ? How are authenticity and recognition negotiated when expressions of self may be generated or curated by AI? Whose languages and ways of life become recognizable, and whose are obscured? All four panels welcome submissions from scholars, students, activists, and independent researchers working in communication and media studies, sociology, political economy, science and technology studies, information studies, cultural studies, area studies, and other related fields. Submissions are open to contributors at all career stages, but we encourage work from early-career scholars and those whose work may sit outside conventional academic structures. Submissions may take the form of a traditional paper, both theoretical and empirical, or adopt a more multimedia/modal approach. Submission Guidelines: Paper Submissions: We invite panelists to submit an extended abstract of no more than 800 words, outlining how their project relates to the symposium, as well as their methods, findings and theoretical contributions. Please include your name, affiliation, a short 100-word biography, and the specific panel to which you are interested in applying. Multimedia and Hybrid Submissions: Please submit an abstract of 800 words explaining how your piece relates to the symposium theme. For multimedia works, explain how text and other elements interact. Please include your name, affiliation, a short 100-word biography, and the specific panel to which you are interested in applying. Please send all submission materials to globallycontestedimaginaries@gmail.com by 5:00PM on December 3rd, 2026. The organizing committee will notify panelists of decisions by January 15th, 2027. If accepted, panelists will be expected to submit a full paper or project by early March. Finished multimedia submission should include a link to the project when relevant. After submission of the final project, panelists will present their work at the symposium on April 8th-9th at the Annenberg School for Communication at the University of Pennsylvania. Partial travel funding may be available for invited panelists who qualify pending budget availability.

items.title: CFP: The Artificial Body: Cyborgs, Clones and Humanoids in Literature and Media
items.excerpt: CALL FOR PAPERS The Artificial Body: Cyborgs, Clones and Humanoids in Literature and Media Edited by ?rem Atasoy and Habib Tekin The edited volume The Artificial Body: Cyborgs, Clones and Humanoids in Literature and Media seeks to explore representations and conceptualizations of artificial, technologically modified, replicated, and human-like bodies from...
items.fullDescription: CALL FOR PAPERS The Artificial Body: Cyborgs, Clones and Humanoids in Literature and Media Edited by ?rem Atasoy and Habib Tekin The edited volume The Artificial Body: Cyborgs, Clones and Humanoids in Literature and Media seeks to explore representations and conceptualizations of artificial, technologically modified, replicated, and human-like bodies from interdisciplinary perspectives. Rather than approaching the artificial body merely as a product of technological development, the volume considers it as a cultural and semiotic site through which changing ideas of embodiment, identity, agency, consciousness, corporeality, and human-machine relations are negotiated. Cyborgs, clones, androids, humanoid robots, synthetic beings, technologically augmented humans, and other forms of artificial or hybrid embodiment have long occupied the cultural imagination. Their representations raise fundamental questions concerning the limits of the human: Where does the human body end and the artificial begin? What happens to identity when the body can be modified, replicated, reconstructed, or manufactured? How do artificial bodies challenge established distinctions between subject and object, organism and machine, self and other? And how do literature and media participate in constructing, questioning, or transforming these boundaries? Situated at the intersections of literary studies, media studies, cultural studies, semiotics, philosophy, and posthumanist and transhumanist thought, the volume welcomes both theoretical contributions and analyses of individual or comparative works. Possible topics include, but are not limited to: · cyborgs and hybrid embodiment · clones, replication, and biological identity · humanoids, androids, and human-like artificial beings · artificial bodies and posthuman subjectivity · transhumanism and technological enhancement · human-machine boundaries · embodiment and artificial intelligence · synthetic and technologically constructed bodies · body modification and augmentation · artificial bodies and questions of identity, memory, and consciousness · the body as sign and the semiotics of artificial embodiment · gender, sexuality, and artificial bodies · artificial bodies in science fiction and cyberpunk · utopian and dystopian representations of technologically transformed bodies · virtual, digital, and simulated bodies · avatars and disembodied/re-embodied identities · artificial bodies and questions of agency and autonomy · the uncanny, the monstrous, and the artificial human · ethics and politics of creating, modifying, and replicating bodies · historical transformations in representations of artificial humans Contributions may examine literary texts, films, television series, graphic narratives, video games, digital narratives, or other relevant media and may employ approaches from literary and cultural studies, media and film studies, semiotics, multimodality, narratology, posthumanism, transhumanism, critical theory, gender studies, or related fields. The volume will be published as part of Interdisciplinary Studies on Philology by Maurer Press, an interdisciplinary series bringing philological research into dialogue with contemporary approaches from literary, linguistic, cultural, media, and related fields. Submission Guidelines Abstract length: 300-500 words Include: title, author name, affiliation, ORCID Formatting: Times New Roman, 12 pt, 1.5 line spacing Abstract submission deadline: December 4, 2026 CPC: The CPC for publication in this volume is 150 Euro per chapter. Publisher: Maurer Press, Germany Important Notes Full chapter length, style sheet, and timeline will be communicated upon abstract acceptance. All submissions should be original and not under consideration elsewhere. The editors and publisher reserve the right to make final selections based on peer review and fit with the volume. Please send abstracts and inquiries to: irem.atasoy@istanbul.edu.tr and habib.tekin@marmara.edu.tr

items.excerpt: Call for Chapters: One Stitch at a Time: Telling Stories, Archiving Histories, and Threading Narratives of Resistance and Rebellion through Embroidered Art and Needlecraft For thousands of years, embroidery and embroidered work have been used as a mode of visual storytelling and of documenting national or cultural histories. From the 12000 years-old fiber...
items.fullDescription: Call for Chapters: One Stitch at a Time: Telling Stories, Archiving Histories, and Threading Narratives of Resistance and Rebellion through Embroidered Art and Needlecraft For thousands of years, embroidery and embroidered work have been used as a mode of visual storytelling and of documenting national or cultural histories. From the 12000 years-old fiberwork found in the Guitarrero Cave, to twine textile artwork of the Peruvian Norte Chico civilization of 2500 BCE, the thousands of years old Chinese silk thread embroidery, the decorative thread arts of the Indus Valley Civilization of 3000 BCE, the ancient Egyptian needlework of 1300 BCE, the Bayeux Tapestry of Norman conquest, and the thousands of years old embroidery and quilt work of the indigenous communities across the North and South Americas, human civilizations have woven and embroidered their histories and cultures and have archived everything for future generations. Embroidery has also functioned as a powerful trope of resistance narrative and rebellious vision. Marjorie Agosín's iconic book, Tapestries of Hope recounts how Chilean women used embroidery and textile art as tools of resistance and rebellion during Pinochet's dictatorship. More recently, Kirstie McLeod's collaborative project "The Red Dress" brings together the needlework, voices, and stories of 380 individuals from 51 countries. Collectively, their embroidered experiences on a single red dress, across a range of expertise, positions, and languages, testify to human rights concerns around the world. In the context of underprivileged women from the global South, embroidery and needlework have been a source of financial freedom and a platform for women's social bonding and personal expressions. For example, cottage industries in Bangladesh, India, and many other South and East Asian countries have mobilized economically impoverished women into an active workforce and have turned embroidery and needlework into a booming business. In literature and media, embroidered works also provide intense narrative power. Adrienne Rich's "Aunt Jennifer's Tigers" and Rosa del Valle's tablecloth in Isabel Allende's The House of the Spirits, are two such examples. Embroidery has provided a pertinent motif for re-presenting folklore, myth, and collective memory in many countries, such as Bangladesh and India, where women's acts of illustrating folklores, personal loss and pain in quilts or narrating the mythical stories of the Ramayana and the Mahabharata through needlework are an essential part of their national and cultural history. Textile arts, embroidery and needlework function as narrative technologies that initiate individual, social, and political involvement. It invokes memory and provokes individuals to make or break myths regarding nation, narration, gender, identity, and/or human existence in the age of artificial intelligence. Against this extensive backdrop of embroidery as a narrative technology, we invite abstracts for a collection tentatively titled One Stitch at a Time: Telling Stories, Archiving Histories, and Threading Narratives of Resistance and Rebellion through Embroidered Art and Needlecraft. Tentative topic list for the paper (but is not limited to): Archiving history through embroidery Embroidery as narrative technology Embroidery as a trope of Agency and/or Identity Embroidery as a narrative of political resistance Embroidery as Storytelling Embroidery and human rights or social justice Embroidery and activism Embroidery and/in literature Embroidery and/as cultural identity Embroidery and/as visual narrative Embroidery and ecocriticism Myth, memory, and embroidery Retelling myth and re-presenting identity Women and embroidery Please send us your 150 words abstract with 3 key words and a 50-word bio by December 10, 2026. If accepted, we will request for the completed essay (minimum of 7000 words) by June 30, 2027. The anthology is expected to be published by a university press in the US. Looking forward to receiving your abstract at fayeza.hasanat@ucf.edu , cc farrah.cato@ucf.edu Sincerely, Dr. Fayeza Hasanat and Dr. Farrah Cato English Department University of Central Florida

items.fullDescription: Social Inclusion, peer-reviewed journal indexed in the Social Sciences Citation Index and Scopus, welcomes new and exciting research papers for its upcoming issue "Inclusive Diversity in European Education: From Policy Frameworks to Classroom Practices," edited by Roberto Baelo Álvarez, Alessandro Bergamaschi, and Anna Elia. Submission of Abstracts: 1-15 December 2026 Submission of Full Papers: 15-30 April 2027 Publication of the Issue: June/December 2027 About the issue: Contemporary European societies are characterised by an unprecedented degree of diversity (linguistic, cultural, ethnic, religious, and socioeconomic), challenging the foundations of traditional educational systems. The concept of superdiversity, which moves beyond binary majority-minority frameworks to account for the complex intersectionality of identities and trajectories, reflects the lived reality of classrooms, schools, and universities across the continent. However, educational policies and pedagogical practices have often lagged behind this transformation, generating tensions between normative aspirations for inclusion and the structural conditions shaping everyday educational contexts. This thematic issue brings together interdisciplinary scholarship examining how educational systems across Europe and beyond are responding, or failing to respond, to the challenges and opportunities posed by diversity. Drawing on sociology, educational science, political science, and intercultural studies, the issue addresses four interconnected dimensions: the normative and policy frameworks governing diversity in education; the social implications of superdiversity for educational communities, particularly the tension between demands for equality and differentiation in everyday school situations; the pedagogical approaches, teacher education strategies, and curricular innovations aimed at fostering inclusive learning environments; and the perspectives of key actors, including students, educators, institutions, and civil society. Finally, the issue aims to critically examine whether inclusion can be considered a new paradigm for understanding social cohesion, alongside established models such as multiculturalism and assimilationism, and their respective contributions to the educational field. The issue welcomes original research, systematic reviews, and theoretically grounded contributions that engage with multiculturalism, intercultural education, diversity management, social cohesion, and inclusive educational practice in formal and non-formal settings across all educational levels. Comparative, cross-national, and transdisciplinary perspectives are particularly encouraged, as are contributions documenting good practices and innovative approaches. By bringing these conversations into dialogue, this issue advances scholarly understanding and evidence-based policy reflection on one of the most pressing challenges facing European and global educational systems today. Instructions for authors: Authors interested in submitting a paper for this issue are asked to consult the journal's instructions for authors and submit their abstracts (maximum of 250 words, with a tentative title) through the abstracts system: https://www.cogitatiopress.com/app/socialinclusion/abstracts When submitting their abstracts, authors are also asked to confirm that they are aware that Social Inclusion is an open access journal with a publishing fee if the article is accepted for publication after peer-review (corresponding authors affiliated with our institutional members do not incur this fee). Open access: Readers across the globe will be able to access, share, and download this issue entirely for free. Corresponding authors affiliated with any of our institutional members (over 100 institutions worldwide) publish free of charge. Otherwise, an article processing fee will be charged to the authors to cover editorial costs. We defend that authors should not have to personally pay this fee and encourage them to check with their institutions if funds are available to cover open access publication costs. Further information about the journal's open access charges can be found here: https://www.cogitatiopress.com/socialinclusion/about/editorialPolicies#publicationFees Abstracts welcome until 15 December 2026.

items.fullDescription: In her book Bodyminds Reimagined , Sami Schalk asks us “What might it mean to imagine disability differently?” (2) Her work, situated in the exploration of black speculative fiction, engages with (dis)ability studies and black feminism to gesture toward a reimagining of what Margaret Price termed the ‘bodymind’, a concept predicated on “the enmeshment of the mind and body.” (5) How might this enmeshment be understood in the context of chronic conditions, themselves experienced as a direct result of climate change and biomedical violence? Is the planet - made sick by extractive capitalism and anthropogenic action as Shukla, Settee, Lincoln and others claim - now existing in a state of (dis)ability?

items.title: [Edited book] Handbook of National Revolutions. National Revolutions in the World: Theories, Practices, International Relations
items.excerpt: Beginning in the nineteenth century, the world witnessed the emergence of national movements that advocated the construction of states founded upon the historical and cultural identity of peoples, as well as upon their independence and strategic autonomy. This wave, which manifested itself most prominently in the European revolutions of 1848, the so-calle...
items.fullDescription: Beginning in the nineteenth century, the world witnessed the emergence of national movements that advocated the construction of states founded upon the historical and cultural identity of peoples, as well as upon their independence and strategic autonomy. This wave, which manifested itself most prominently in the European revolutions of 1848, the so-called "Springtime of the Peoples," produced a long-term historical impact - according to the principle of the longue durée - that influenced world political history in the decades that followed. This phenomenon was of enormous importance in the Western political sphere, having its precursors in the American Revolution and in the political epic of South American Bolivarianism, and gaining momentum from 1848 onward with the emergence of a whole series of European national movements. With the First World War, and with the promotion by Woodrow Wilson and the United States of the principle of "self-determination of peoples," the same idea experienced a revival which, through Turkish Kemalism and the formation of the Chinese nationalist movement, extended into the non-Western world. Non-Western forms of this type of movement, in turn, had important precursors in anti-colonial movements, which, like European national movements, sought to secure independence and autonomy for broad sectors of the world subjected to foreign domination of an economic and extractive nature. During the twentieth century, the idea of national independence assumed various ideological and political forms, eventually giving rise to different theories of national autonomy and sovereignty, such as Mao Zedong's "Three Worlds Theory." At the same time, the rise of communist revolutions and of the world socialist camp revitalized this political idea, generating new formulations of theories of national revolution. With this call for papers, we intend to collect contributions on the theme of national revolutions in the West and the East, considered both from a theoretical perspective - by examining the political thought of the authors who promoted these movements, as well as the movements themselves - and from the perspective of the relations among these movements and the elaboration of a political theory of coexistence among these political projects. We also intend to focus on the theories and practices of these movements from the perspective of international relations, both by analyzing national revolutions within the international context, in diplomatic and strategic terms, and by addressing the theoretical elaboration of an international order founded upon national independence. A non-exhaustive list of topics that may be addressed includes: Jacobinism and the emergence of the idea of national revolution in Europe The American Revolution and the national-revolutionary paradigm Bolivarianism and national revolution in Spanish America 1848 and the transformation of the national idea in Europe Mazzini and the theory of nationalities The Italian Risorgimento and its relationship with the great powers Bonapartism and national revolutions Self-determination of peoples and the international order after the First World War Kemalism and the Turkish national revolutionù The Soviet Revolution and the issue of nationalities Chinese nationalism and national revolution in the thought of Sun Yat-sen Nationalism and anti-imperialism in anti-colonial liberation movements Mao Zedong and the theory of national revolution National revolution and internationalism in Marxist and communist thought National sovereignty, the balance of power, and the international order National identity and international relations theory National movements and the opposition to a bipolar and unipolar world National movements and anti-colonial struggles in Africa Arab nationalism and movements for emancipation in the Middle East Indian nationalism and the struggle for independence National and revolutionary movements in twentieth-century Latin America Nationalisms in Southeast Asia and the dissolution of the colonial empire Proposals should contain a title, a brief summary or abstract of between 300 and 400 words, the author's email address, and a brief five-line CV. Proposals must be sent to the email address nationalrevolutionsintheworld@gmail.com The deadline for submitting proposals is December 31, 2026. Accepted proposals will be announced starting January 31, 2027, and editorial instructions for preparing the book chapter will be provided. The deadline for submitting the final version of the chapters will be a date to be determined in the first quarter of 2027. The monograph containing the selected and submitted book chapters will subsequently be published, following corrections and comments by the coordinators. The monograph is expected to be published by an international academic publishing house. Coordinators: Orazio Maria Gnerre (Institute for the History of the Italian Risorgimento) Ruikai Xue (Beijing International Studies University)

It focuses on the comprehensive discourse of games and digital games, including theoretical and empirical studies, research results, and their implementation into practice, as well as professional publication reviews and scientific reviews of digital games. Acta Ludologica is inviting manuscripts for Vol. 10, No. 1 , scheduled to be published in June 2027. The deadline for submissions is December 31, 2026 . Journal issues include scientific reflections on digital and non-digital games, and related media and digital competencies, their creation, design, development, research, history, sociology, psychology, marketing, and the future associated with phenomena of the digital-gaming sector. The journal' regular issues are not thematically oriented, so this CFP is general for manuscripts on any topics related to games and digital games. Acta Ludologica's sections: game studies, reviews, add-ons More information about the individual journal sections, instructions for authors, as well as templates are available in the journal's Guidelines (https://actaludologica.com/guidelines/). Submitted manuscripts should strictly follow the outlined format as well as the journal's Citation Rules. Submissions are accepted only in English, with no publication fees, article-processing charges (APCs), or article submission charges. items.fullDescription: How is everyone doing? At a routine meeting of the Editorial Board of this journal in March 2026, this innocuous question erupted into disquiet, tension, unease. Speaking from vastly different parts of the world, there was an unmistakable sense of a planet slipping beyond available comprehension and unplugging us from work and life routines. As wars in the Middle East expand and fires spread from apartment blocks reduced to rubble to bombed oil refineries and shipping corridors, profound geopolitical, personal, even psychic rifts leave us grasping for the language and feel of the moment, the falling apart of things, the zeitgeist of an endangered now.

items.title: Animal Studies Across Disciplines
items.location: Arizona State University · Arizona State University
items.excerpt: Animal Studies Across Disciplines Symposium April 7th-April 9th 2027 Arizona State University Many scholars argue that we are now living in a new geological epoch-the Anthropocene-a name chosen to encapsulate an irreversibly transformed planet due to the rapid expansion of human populations, increasing exploitation of animals and natural resources, and pe...
items.fullDescription: Animal Studies Across Disciplines Symposium April 7th-April 9th 2027 Arizona State University Many scholars argue that we are now living in a new geological epoch-the Anthropocene-a name chosen to encapsulate an irreversibly transformed planet due to the rapid expansion of human populations, increasing exploitation of animals and natural resources, and pervasive pollution. The effects of the Anthropocene have been caused by only a small percentage of the world's population, yet those living in the Global South disproportionately suffer the consequences. The Anthropocene, then, is just as much a social problem as it is an environmental issue. Despite the centrality of animals to planetary health, however, nonhuman life often remains peripheral to discussions of climate and environmental sustainability, even as industrial agriculture drives deforestation and carbon emissions, species extinction destabilizes ecosystems, and the increasing emergence of zoonotic diseases-Covid-19 and Hantavirus among them-reveals the profound interdependence of human, animal, and environmental health. At the same time, dominant responses to environmental crises, which made possible the conditions of crisis in the first place, tend to privilege scientific discovery and technological innovation while neglecting the cultural narratives, entrenched biases, and networks of power that shape human-animal relationships.. To that end, imagining more just and hospitable futures requires new interdisciplinary approaches that recognize animals and interspecies relations as critical to collective flourishing and environmental sustainability. The Animal Studies Across Disciplines Symposium will bring together scholars, artists, students, animal professionals, and community members across the humanities, social sciences, and natural sciences to discuss animals and multispecies futures. The symposium is designed not only as a scholarly gathering, but as the start of a long-term collaborative network capable of shaping future research, public humanities work, community partnerships, and environmental dialogue. The inaugural Spring 2027 Symposium will center on the keyword "care," inviting participants to analyze how different disciplines, professions, and communities define and mobilize care in relation to animals, multispecies justice, and environmental stewardship. In doing so, the Symposium will evaluate practices of protection and responsibility alongside the violences and inequalities that shape life across species. For example, how might a humanities scholar, veterinarian, ecologist, or activist understand and practice care differently, and what might each learn from the knowledge, methods, and questions of the others? How might regional, place-based, and communal forms of knowledge offer different ways of understanding our relationships and responsibilities to animals? How is care negotiated when the welfare of an individual animal comes into conflict with the preservation of a population, species, or ecosystem? What might care mean for animals such as insects, whose small size, vast numbers, and frequent classification as pests or disease vectors complicate familiar practices of care? How do animals care for themselves, one another, and members of other species, and what might these practices teach us about caring for each other and the more-than-human world? The Symposium invites participants to consider what becomes possible when different ways of knowing and relating to animals are brought into conversation, and how such exchanges might expand our understanding and practice of care across species. items.title: Derrick Bell and the History of Africana Philosophy
items.excerpt: The Journal for the New Narratives in the History of Philosophy (JNNHP) invites submissions for its special on Derrick Bell and the History of Africana Philosophy, to be published in Fall 2027. Derrick Bell, the founder of Critical Race Theory, produced one of the most innovative, insightful, and transformative ideas in the 20th century. His philosophical...
items.fullDescription: The Journal for the New Narratives in the History of Philosophy (JNNHP) invites submissions for its special on Derrick Bell and the History of Africana Philosophy, to be published in Fall 2027. Derrick Bell, the founder of Critical Race Theory, produced one of the most innovative, insightful, and transformative ideas in the 20th century. His philosophical insights continue to challenge how western liberal nations contend with questions of civil rights, human rights, immigration, policing, and education. Recent conservative attacks focused on Critical Race Theory (CRT) in the U.S, Canada, and England assert, albeit erroneously, that CRT is a Marxist and communist ideology that seeks to supplant western values and the ethos of liberal democracy. Contrary to these fallacious attacks, Bell's textbook Race, Racism, and American Law is amongst the first law textbooks to give a comprehensive view of how racism shaped the development of American law and race relations. In this regard, CRT draws heavily on a tradition of Africana philosophy from slavery through the 20th century. It challenges, not only the supposed neutrality of U.S. law, but also the universality of western political ideals, and U.S. law as egalitarian. For example, Bell engaged Frederick Douglass's critiques of natural law theorists and abolitionists who read the American Constitution as a slave document. For Douglass, the Constitution is an economic contract that robs slaves of their labour and property rights. Drawing on Douglass' critique, Bell interrogated how economic interests have structured American law as an instrument for white class interests over Black claims for justice from slavery through the 20th century. Similarly, Bell engaged W.E.B DuBois's reading of American democracy that underscored how U.S. law in the 13 colonies suppressed African revolts while upholding slavery. Such legal resistance to African acts of liberation, Dubois argued, created paradoxes for American democracy and shaped how the legal system understood the Black freedom struggle. Following Dubois' analysis, Bell explored how the law is an ineffective tool for racial remediation when it comes to addressing social injustices that confront Black life. Bell also engaged Malcolm X's critiques of the Reconstruction era civil rights and 1960 civil rights amendments as pyrrhic victories. This inspired Bell to think about how civil rights function as symbolic victories while ensuring racism is a permanent fixture of American democracy. Given Bell's extensive engagement with 18th-20th century Africana philosophy, this special seeks to consider Bell's work within Africana philosophy. As such, the special welcomes essays that focus on Bell's work as philosophical historiography and inquiry into Black life and its relation to democracy as part of the long tradition of Africana philosophy. The special seeks contributions that address the following themes: Derrick Bell as a philosopher of Black history. Derrick Bell as a philosopher of Black legal theory. Derrick Bell and the Black Nationalist and the Black Radical Tradition. Derrick Bell as a philosopher of Black Education. Derrick Bell as a philosopher of contemporary society and issue of civil rights. Essays must be submitted to https://journal.lib.uoguelph.ca/index.php/nnhp/about/submissions Deadline for Essay Submission: January 7th, 2027. Papers will be considered after January 7th, 2027. The Co-lead Guest Editors for this Special are Drs. Dalitso Ruwe (Queens University), Adebayo Oluwayomi (West Chester University), Andrew Soto (Hartnell College). For questions about the Special, please contact: derrickbellspecial@gmail.com JNNHP is an open-access online journal committed to publishing papers on underrepresented figures or themes in the history of philosophy, both Western and non-Western traditions, from the ancient period to the mid-20th century. JNNHP accepts papers in English and French. Papers should be no more than 10000 words. JNNHP also seeks to highlight relevant translations, archival work or new editions of primary texts in progress. We will publish selections from such works, with critical notes and contextual introductions.
