items.location: Vrije Universiteit Brussel (Brussels, Belgium) · Vrije Universiteit Brussel
items.excerpt: CALL FOR PAPERS Affective Worlds: Emotions and Aesthetics in Afro-Descendant Women's Writing International Conference 24-25 May 2027, Vrije Universiteit Brussel (Belgium) Format: in person Language: English Link to the CfP : https://clic.research.vub.be/afropemotions-international-conference The conference explores the role of affect, emotions, and aesthe...
items.fullDescription: CALL FOR PAPERS Affective Worlds: Emotions and Aesthetics in Afro-Descendant Women's Writing International Conference 24-25 May 2027, Vrije Universiteit Brussel (Belgium) Format: in person Language: English Link to the CfP : https://clic.research.vub.be/afropemotions-international-conference The conference explores the role of affect, emotions, and aesthetics in the rich and diverse body of work published in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries by women writers of African heritage from African, European, Caribbean, and other diasporic contexts. The event examines how affect and emotions shape both the sociopolitical dimensions of Afro-descendant women's literature and its narrative and aesthetic practices across multiple linguistic, cultural, and historical contexts and through fiction, poetry, and drama. By often exploring issues of displacement, marginalisation, systemic oppression, colonial legacies, trauma, cultural memory, and environmental change, Afro-descendant women authors present affect as a site of self-awareness, resistance, community formation, and political imagination, while articulating it through narrative form, language, imagery, and other aesthetic strategies. The conference brings together established and early-career researchers working at the intersection of different fields, including affect studies, African and African diasporic literary studies, comparative literary studies, feminist and queer studies, postcolonial and decolonial studies, trauma and cultural memory studies, and the environmental humanities. While acknowledging theoretical distinctions between affect and emotion, particularly those developed in affect theory by scholars such as Tomkins (1962) and Massumi (2002), the conference welcomes literary criticism informed by diverse affective frameworks, such as cognitive and narratological perspectives on affect (e.g. Hogan 2003, 2011), sociopolitical approaches to affect and emotions (e.g. Ahmed 2004; Berlant 2011), and affective ecocriticism (e.g. Bladow and Ladino 2018). We invite papers exploring affect and emotions in Afro-descendant women's literature written in English, French, German, Italian, or other languages. Topics may include but are not limited to: Affective relations, transnational belonging, and diasporic identities Migration, displacement, and affective literary geographies Affect and gender, race, class, and sexuality Queer affects Affect, narrative form, and aesthetics Affect, language, multilingualism, and translation Emotions, trauma, and memory Collective affect, solidarity, and community formation Eco-emotions and environmental change Emotional responses to injustice, inequality, and systemic oppression Affect, embodiment, and resistance SUBMISSION GUIDELINES Please send proposals for 20-minute papers in English to Dr. Isabella Villanova (Isabella.Villanova@vub.be) and Prof. dr. Elisabeth Bekers (Elisabeth.Bekers@vub.be). Proposals should include: an abstract (max. 250 words), with up to 5 references, preferably in Chicago style; 5 keywords; a short biographical note (max. 100 words) Deadline for Proposal Submissions: 10 January 2027 Notification of Acceptance: 10 February 2027 Selected papers may be considered for publication in a special journal issue. Keynote: Prof. dr. Caroline Kögler (Freie Universität Berlin, Germany) Special Guest: Italo-Somali writer Ubah Cristina Ali Farah

items.fullDescription: Call for Proposals The editorial and scientific board of the journal Co-herencia invites researchers, professors, and scholars affiliated with national or international institutions to submit proposals for thematic issues/dossiers, and to apply to serve as Guest Scientific Editors for Volume 25, Issue 48 (covering the period January-June 2028). Presentation and Scientific Scope of the Journal Co-herencia Co-herencia is an indexed scientific journal, published biannually, under Diamond Open Access with a CC BY 4.0 license, and edited by the School of Arts and Humanities at EAFIT University. Indexed in major international databases such as Scopus (Arts & Humanities, Q2 SJR), Co-herencia ensures methodological rigor, double-blind peer review, and high ethical publishing standards. The journal is published in Spanish, English, and Portuguese. Published without interruption since 2004, the journal aims to serve as a forum for interdisciplinary discussion on the contributions of the humanities and the arts to the shaping of a thoughtful, critical, and deliberative community. Its scope and thematic axes are concentrated mainly on: Literary Studies: Literary theory; Literary genres; Classical tradition; Hermeneutics; Canon, criticism, and history of literature in the Americas; Writing and orality; Translation; Reception; Literary creation; Semiotics; Editing studies; Journalism and literature; Applied literature. Philosophical Studies: Critical theory and social philosophy; Ethics; Political philosophy; Aesthetics; Epistemology; Philosophy of science and technology; Philosophy of mind; Cosmology; Philosophy of language; Argumentation theory; Rhetoric; Phenomenology; Philosophical hermeneutics; Ontology; Conceptual analysis; History of philosophy. Historical Studies: Historiography; Theory and philosophy of history; Methodology of history; Intellectual history; Conceptual history; Cultural history; Social and political history; History of knowledge; National and Latin American history; Global history; Colonial history; Memory and history; Historical geography and cartography; Imagination, speculation, and historical narratives. Arts: Mediality, transmediality, and intermediality; Creative industries; Musicology; History of music; Material and visual culture; Curatorship and museography; Sociology of the arts; Interartistic relations; Avant-gardes and artistic movements; Canon, criticism, and history of the arts in the Americas. Humanistic Studies in Dialogue with the Social Sciences: Critical discourse analysis; Plain language; Digital humanities; Cultural studies; Research-Creation; Philosophical and historical anthropology; Human geography; Environmental humanities; Medical humanities; Digital humanities; Public humanities; Qualitative analysis of quantitative methods; Clinical sociology; Studies on violence, peace, and reconciliation; Communication studies with a humanistic approach; Gender studies. Requirements for Submitting Proposals In keeping with international editorial best practices in the field of Arts and Humanities (diverse impact, editorial exogamy, international outreach, and analytical rigor), proposals submitted by candidates for guest editors must be presented in a single document (PDF or Word), written in Spanish, English, or Portuguese, and must include, in detail, the following five sections: Title of the thematic issue: it should be concise, clear, conceptually strong, and reflect the central problem to be addressed. Thematic presentation and theoretical grounding (500 to 1,000 words): propose a conceptual delimitation and a definition of the object of study, the core question, or the problematizing axis of the dossier. The proposal should also detail the disciplinary or interdisciplinary frameworks, indicating how the theme and approach engage with the journal's scientific scope. Justification and academic relevance (500 to 1,000 words): include a synthesis of the state of the art and a clear account of the novelty and relevance of the proposal within the contemporary debate in the arts and humanities. This section should ideally state the potential impact and interest the issue will generate within the international research community. Scientific biography of the prospective guest editors: a team of two to three guest editors with diverse institutional affiliations is recommended. For each team member, please indicate: full name, current institutional affiliation, highest academic degree, ORCID iD, and a summary (max. 300 words) of their research lines, ongoing projects, and recent publications in the thematic area of the proposal. List of prospective authors and articles: as evidence of the commitment to attracting original manuscripts, this section of the proposal must list between 3 and 6 potential or pre-invited authors of recognized standing or relevant emerging trajectory for the thematic issue. For each anticipated contribution, please provide: the author's full name, institutional affiliation, tentative article title, and a brief abstract (100-200 words). All manuscripts resulting from the call for the selected proposal must undergo double-blind peer review. Guest editors commit to actively participating in the preselection of manuscripts, suggesting qualified reviewers, and drafting a presentation/introduction for the dossier. Timeline for the Open Call and the Editorial Process Opening of the call for thematic issue proposals: September 1, 2026. Deadline for submission of thematic issue proposals: January 10, 2027. Evaluation of proposals by the scientific board and notification of results: January 25, 2027. Public launch of the call for the selected proposal: January 31, 2027. Deadline for submission of articles for the thematic dossier: May 31, 2027. Peer review and revision process: June-November 2027. Early publication of revised articles: October 2027-January 2028. Copyediting, XML-JATS markup, and digital layout: November 2027-February 2028. Official publication (Vol. 25, No. 48, January-June 2028): February-March 2028. How to Submit Proposals Complete proposals must be submitted electronically to the journal's official email (co-herencia@eafit.edu.co) or processed through the Co-herencia journal's OJS (Open Journal System) platform, attaching the document (PDF or Word) with the required information, using the subject line "Application for Thematic Dossier Vol. 25-48 - [Short title of the proposal]." Contacts for Further Information Editorial team of the journal Co-herencia: coherencia@eafit.edu.co Editorial assistant: Liam Agudelo Calle lagudeloc@eafit.edu.co Editor-in-chief: Andrés Vélez-Posada avelezp6@eafit.edu.co

Breaking off a glacier located high on the Langtang Lirung peak in Nepal's Langtang National Park, the flood consumed everything in its path in a spectacle of destruction. items.location: Mobile, Alabama · University of South Alabama
items.excerpt: Call for Papers: "Loving Roland Barthes" University of South Alabama (Mobile, AL) October 14-16, 2027 Loving [Barthes], doing so in a certain fashion against the age [. . .], can only be a responsible way of living: it inevitably leads the subject who does so and says so to posit himself in his time according to the injunctions of his desire and not accor...
items.fullDescription: Call for Papers: "Loving Roland Barthes" University of South Alabama (Mobile, AL) October 14-16, 2027 Loving [Barthes], doing so in a certain fashion against the age [. . .], can only be a responsible way of living: it inevitably leads the subject who does so and says so to posit himself in his time according to the injunctions of his desire and not according to those of his sociality. -Roland Barthes, "Loving Schumann" Proposals for panels and papers are invited for a conference entitled "Loving Roland Barthes: Celebrating the Fiftieth Anniversary of the Publication of A Lover's Discourse: Fragments ," to be hosted by the University of South Alabama's Department of English and held at the historic Malaga Inn in downtown Mobile, city of the oldest Mardi Gras in the U.S. As conference organizers, we envision a relatively concentrated event in which scholars working in various disciplines and artists working in various genres will present new ideas about Roland Barthes, A Lover's Discourse , and his adjacent texts. This conference celebrates a peculiar form of love: an amorousness that compels the one faithful to "the specialty of [one's] desire" ( Lover's Discourse 20) to return again and again to Fragments d'un discours amoureux . Published in 1977 and translated a year later by Richard Howard as A Lover's Discourse: Fragments , Roland Barthes's tortured love song retains a strong attachment for scholars and artists alike. We might be tempted to call those strange lovers "amateurs." For, as Barthes reminded us, the word derives from "amator: one who loves and loves again" (Roland Barthes 52). Across the last five decades, the book has inspired not only articles and artwork but also autotheory, "an emergent discourse with historical precedents" (McLaughlin et al., Autotheory and Its Others 15). Often recognizable by its copious citations, autotheoretical practice pays homage to A Lover's Discourse: Fragments as one way of loving Barthes. Yet there is no limit to the modes of loving Barthes. For some, it might be collage, an assemblage of the very fragments that Barthes favored. For others, it might be singing a song (such as Annie Lennox's "No More 'I Love You's'") or writing notations (one of Barthes's preferred activities). For still others, it might be searching for "a little corner of sloth," "twiddl[ing one's] wound," or accepting "[t]he lover's fatal identity [. . .]: I am the one who waits" (Lover's Discourse 64, 161, 40). Whatever one's manner of loving Barthes, this conference invites scholars and artists to a celebration of A Lover's Discourse: Fragments . Contributions can take the form of traditional papers as well as of visual art, short film, skits, songs, and other Barthesian types of work or play. Possible topics include but are not limited to the following: · Figures and images in A Lover's Discourse: Fragments ; · Fragments and citations; · "[C]ontrolled accident" ("An Almost Obsessive Relation to Writing Instruments" 182) and the text's other structural and organizational features; · Barthes's use of Goethe's Werther; · "[T]he history of tears," "a scenography of waiting," and other extrapolations from the text (180, 37); · Relationships between this text and other works by Barthes, especially from the 1970s; · Barthes's (post)structuralist discussions of substitution, replication, and supplement; · Translation and differences between the French and English versions of the text; · Autotheory and other experimental, creative-critical practices inspired by Barthes; · (Loving) parodies of A Lover's Discourse ; · Anachronism in A Lover's Discourse both at the point of publication and now. As much as we trust that this conference will generate exciting new art and scholarship, we also hope to foster a substantial exchange of ideas and perspectives among all participants as well as personal interaction among scheduled presentations. Therefore, conference panels will be scheduled sequentially rather than concurrently so that all participants will be able to attend all panels, and we strongly encourage participants to stay for the duration of the conference. We believe that much good work will come from the conference, and we hope to assemble a collection of that work in the months following the conference in order to share it with the widest possible audience. Kicking off the conference will be a keynote address by Tufts professor John Lurz, author of The Barthes Fantastic: Literature, Criticism, and the Practice of Language . Please submit proposals of 350-500 words by email to Becky McLaughlin (email address: bmclaugh@southalabama.edu) and Eric Daffron (email address: edaffron@ramapo.edu) or by snail mail to Becky McLaughlin, Department of English, HUMB 240, University of South Alabama, Mobile, AL 36688. Due date: January 15, 2027.

items.fullDescription: CALL FOR PAPERS First International Congress in Humanities - Texts, Images and Communities: "Body, Age and Gender" Org. HUM-TIC Research Group, University of Madeira, 17-18 June 2017 The way in which the body, age and gender shape human experiences is one of the most pressing challenges facing contemporary societies. Today, more than ever, there is a need to build fairer, more equitable and sustainable communities, which are in a state of continuous development and adaptation and which face limitations and obstacles. Some of these are long-standing and deeply rooted, whilst others are new and not very well known. A multidisciplinary approach to the cultural and social constructs of the body - and the multiple levels at which it functions as a generator of meaning - is therefore imperative. The proposed lines of research, both in their contemporary context and in terms of their cultural and historical foundations, fall within the core mission of the Humanities Research Group - Texts, Images and Communities (HUM-TIC). This event fosters free, informed discussion, driven by dialogue across the Humanities. This is the first International Congress organised by the HUM-TIC Research Group, Faculty of Arts and Humanities at the University of Madeira. It is an in-person event, which will take place at the Colégio dos Jesuítas, at the University of Madeira's Rectorate building in Funchal. The conference aims to explore one of HUM-TIC's main thematic areas - Body, Age and Gender - from a dialogical and transdisciplinary perspective. In this context, proposals of a theoretical or empirical nature, including case studies, are welcome across the Humanities. These may include, among others, Art, Communication, Culture, Design, History, Linguistics, Literature, Psychology and Sociology. Discussion Topics (some suggestions): - Discourses, narratives and representations of the body, age and gender. - The body, space and territoriality: real, symbolic and imaginary places. - Rethinking the Human: AI and representations of the body, age and gender. - Aesthetics of the body, beauty and ugliness, the monstrous and the abject. - Building Self and the Other in different cultural contexts. - Stages of life: representations, experiences and intergenerational relationships. - Double standards of ageing in a consumer society. - Embodiment: inner and outer, personal and social, physical and idealised. - Body and gender: sexuality, emotions, ethics, violence. - Myths, stereotypes and imagined representations of the body, age and gender. - Ecologies of the body and environmental humanities. - Gender-based violence in the digital sphere. - The manosphere and social media impact. - Intersectionality and multiple forms of discrimination. - Gender, natural disasters and climate change. items.title: Black Is...Black Is: Story as Construction and Celebration of Identity
items.location: Howard University · The Gregory J. Hampton Graduate English Student Association at Howard University
items.excerpt: In his seminal and final film Black Is…Black Ain't , the documentarian Marlon Riggs utilizes a pot of gumbo to articulate his thesis that Blackness necessitates an identity built on multiplicity, complication, and depth (Riggs 1995). Such a vision contests and destabilizes narratives depicted within the film that sought to limit Black identities an...
items.fullDescription: In his seminal and final film Black Is…Black Ain't , the documentarian Marlon Riggs utilizes a pot of gumbo to articulate his thesis that Blackness necessitates an identity built on multiplicity, complication, and depth (Riggs 1995). Such a vision contests and destabilizes narratives depicted within the film that sought to limit Black identities and identifications, and it cuts against the second half of his title, which suggests Blackness in terms of negation, evasion, and minimization. His articulation becomes not just an evocation of Black identifications but a creation of what a Black identity can be. Riggs continues a conversation with Ralph Ellison, Ama Ata Aidoo, Toni Morrison, Stuart Hall, and centuries of international Black thought. By doubling down on the "is" and considering contradictory, harmonious, and contrapuntal accounts of the many ways Blackness is and can be, the Gregory J. Hampton Graduate English Student Association hopes to join this dialogue with its March 25-26, 2027 conference. We invite papers that contemplate how storytelling produces and shapes Black identities as much as it narrates them, forming, revising, and improvising senses of self and community. This conference also does commemorative work. We are honoring the career of Dr. Jimisha Relerford, a graduate of our program and member of the Howard community who passed recently. Her dissertation broke critical ground in its study of Black women's satire. We thus encourage the submission of papers about Black satire, especially Black women's work in the genre. Writers such as Leone Ross, Danzy Senna, Fran Ross, and Zadie Smith, all of whom were discussed in Dr. Relerford's dissertation, use satire to comment on and transform notions of Blackness. We hope to continue Dr. Relerford's project by reflecting on how storytellers work within this genre to talk about identity. We additionally encourage studies of Afrofuturist and speculative Black texts in reference to our organization's namesake, a pillar in Afrofuturist study. In addition to recognizing the intellectual impacts of Drs. Relerford and Hampton, this conference serves as a milestone, marking the tenth conference our organization has hosted in honor of Black literary study. Given Black academia and HBCUs's influence on identity and storytelling around it, we also welcome papers pondering scholarly impacts on identity as seen in criticism, productions, and protest. We additionally invite papers in the following areas that intersect with identity and identification study in story: African Studies African-American Studies Caribbean Studies Disability Studies Ecocriticism and Ecopoetics Diaspora, Ethnicity, and Migration Studies Food Studies Hip Hop Humor Literary History Protest and Rhetoric Queer Studies Television and Film Theater and Performance To submit a paper or panel to our conference, please email an abstract of 250-300 words to gesasecretary@gmail.com no later than January 15, 2027. In your email include your name, affiliation, contact information, and a brief biographical blurb.

items.title: Frames and Framing: Constructing Meaning in Literature, Linguistics, and Translation
items.location: Faculty of Al-Alsun (Languages), Ain Shams University
items.excerpt: Every act of communication, interpretation, and representation is an act of framing. In literary analysis, a “frame” might define genre, direct narrative perspective, or position a text within a historical moment. In linguistics, frames organize semantic understanding, govern pragmatic interaction, and underpin metaphor. In translation and interpreting, f...
items.fullDescription: Every act of communication, interpretation, and representation is an act of framing. In literary analysis, a “frame” might define genre, direct narrative perspective, or position a text within a historical moment. In linguistics, frames organize semantic understanding, govern pragmatic interaction, and underpin metaphor. In translation and interpreting, frames are negotiated, shifted, and sometimes shattered in the movement between languages and cultures. They are the selective filters that highlight certain elements while relegating others to the background, the conceptual structures that allow us to categorize, interpret, and communicate complex realities.

items.title: “Somewhere in Between: Borders and Borderlands”
items.location: London / Online · London Centre for Interdisciplinary Research
items.excerpt: In an ever changing world the problems of setting boundaries as well as the need to create meanings and establish understanding of diverse phenomena have always been of the utmost importance for humanity. Borders, boundaries, frontiers, and borderlands, naturally formed or man made, are grounded in various ethical traditions, and have always been associat...
items.fullDescription: In an ever changing world the problems of setting boundaries as well as the need to create meanings and establish understanding of diverse phenomena have always been of the utmost importance for humanity. Borders, boundaries, frontiers, and borderlands, naturally formed or man made, are grounded in various ethical traditions, and have always been associated with limits and restrictions. The ongoing process of globalisation is changing the role and stereotypes of borders, so that they are often seen as opportunities rather than constraints. However, in some cases they are still being militarized and conflicted. The conference will seek to identify and analyse the processes of border-making and border permeability in contemporary societies through aesthetic forms. We seek to explore the historical origins of borders, their role in today's global environment and define the notion of borders, which includes not only territorial, geographical, and political borders, but also cultural and metaphorical borders, imagined spaces where interests and ideologies overlap and compete. Conference panels will be related, but not limited, to: border poetics border-crossing security versus openness of borders cultural hybridization cross?border co?operation processes of de?bordering borders and refugees social, cultural or language differences between communities

items.title: Call for Papers in Special Issue “Progress in Thermal Energy Conversion and Storage for Decarbonization: Performance, Flexibility, and Sustainability”
items.excerpt: Dear Colleagues, The transition toward decarbonization and low-carbon energy systems relies not only on scaling up renewable energy but also on improving the conversion, storage, and use of thermal energy. Thermal energy conversion and storage technologies naturally complement one another across both low- and high-temperature ranges: high-efficiency conve...
items.fullDescription: Dear Colleagues, The transition toward decarbonization and low-carbon energy systems relies not only on scaling up renewable energy but also on improving the conversion, storage, and use of thermal energy. Thermal energy conversion and storage technologies naturally complement one another across both low- and high-temperature ranges: high-efficiency conversion systems reduce primary energy use and capture resources that would otherwise be wasted, while storage solutions help match supply with demand, enhance operational flexibility, and support the integration of intermittent renewable sources. Combined, these approaches can increase the efficiency, reliability, and sustainability of electricity, heating, cooling, and industrial operations. Although some advances have been made, several scientific and engineering challenges remain. Key issues involve cutting energy and exergy losses, maintaining performance under part-load and fluctuating operating conditions, boosting storage density, limiting material degradation, enhancing component durability, and enabling cost-effective system integration. Bridging the gap between promising concepts and practical, deployable systems also calls for improved modeling, robust experimental validation, effective scale-up approaches, and transparent benchmarking against existing technologies. This Special Issue (for details, please visit: https://www.mdpi.com/journal/energies/special_issues/YT0537BB7Z) focuses on the recent progress and developments in thermal energy conversion and storage for future decarbonization. Several theoretical, numerical, experimental, and data-driven studies that encompass emerging ideas as well as significant enhancements to established technologies are welcomed. Topics of interest for publication include, but are not limited to, the following: - Advanced and flexible thermodynamic cycles; - Rankine cycle, Brayton cycle, organic Rankine cycle, Kalina cycle, transcritical cycle, supercritical CO2 cycles, and other novel thermodynamic cycles; - Heat pumps, refrigeration, cogeneration, and polygeneration; - Integrated thermal energy conversion and storage system, Carnot battery, heat-to-power system, photothermal energy storage system; - Geothermal, solar-thermal, biomass, and waste-heat recovery systems; - Sensible, latent, and thermochemical energy storage; - Phase-change materials and advanced thermal-storage media; - Working fluids, heat exchangers, volumetric expander/turbine, pump, and thermal-system components; - Integrated and hybrid thermodynamic cycle and thermal storage configurations; - Dynamic, off-design, and part-load performance of thermodynamic cycle and/or thermal storage systems; - Flexible operation and advanced control system for thermodynamic cycle and/or thermal storage systems; - Energy, exergy, economic, and environmental assessments of thermodynamic and/or storage systems; - The use of artificial intelligence, machine learning, surrogate models, LLMs, and digital twins for the advancement of thermal energy conversion and storage systems (for designing, optimizing, controlling, and so on); - Experimental validation, pilot plants, scale-up, demonstration, laboratory test-stand, and industrial applications of thermal energy conversion and storage systems. Although this Special Issue accepts interdisciplinary research spanning mechanical engineering, materials science, and computer science, the core focus of every submitted manuscript must remain within the field of thermal energy conversion, thermal energy storage, or their integration. Manuscripts that primarily address general optimization algorithms, pure environmental life-cycle assessments disconnected from energy performance, or artificial intelligence applications without a substantive and demonstrable link to thermal energy systems are outside the scope of this Special Issue. Dr. Sindu Daniarta Guest Editor

items.fullDescription: CALL FOR PAPERS AND PRESENTATIONS AI AND THE IMAGINATION April 20-23, 2027 Oral Roberts University | Tulsa, Oklahoma, USA Proposal deadline: March 5, 2027 Rolling review; applicants will normally receive a decision within two weeks. In-person presentations only. Featuring Orson Scott Card, award-winning author of Ender's Game and Speaker for the Dead, with keynote speakers Pat Gelsinger, Joan Slonczewski, and Ben John. ABOUT THE CONFERENCE Oral Roberts University invites proposals for AI and the Imagination from participants across disciplines and professions. We welcome research, critical reflection, creative work, and practical applications. Students, faculty, researchers, educators, industry professionals, practitioners, faith leaders, writers, and artists are encouraged to contribute. Artificial intelligence is reshaping how we learn, work, create, and understand ourselves. The conference brings together conversations that too often occur separately, offering an opportunity to share ideas and experiences, question assumptions, and consider how our choices today will shape the years ahead. Interdisciplinary contributions are particularly encouraged. CONFERENCE TRACKS AI and the Imagination How have we imagined artificial intelligence, and how is artificial intelligence changing imagination itself? This signature track welcomes work involving science fiction, fantasy, film, literature, art, storytelling, speculative futures, AI-assisted creativity, and the ways imaginative works can help us understand possible technological futures. AI, Theology, and Ethics What theological, philosophical, and ethical questions arise from increasingly capable artificial intelligence? This track welcomes work on Christian theology and AI, ethics, human dignity, personhood, moral agency, wisdom, responsibility, vocation, technology and faith, and related philosophical or religious questions. AI, Human Agency, and Formation How does AI change what it means to think, choose, act, develop, and become? This track explores human agency in an age of increasingly capable AI, including cognitive and agency offloading, judgment and decision-making, autonomy, dependence, human-AI relationships, meaning, purpose, identity, formation, and human flourishing. AI and Teaching and Learning How is AI changing education and the work of teaching and learning? Topics may include pedagogy, assessment, academic integrity, AI literacy and fluency, faculty development, student learning, educational technology, curriculum design, personalized learning, and emerging models of education. AI, Society, and the Human Future What does widespread AI mean for individuals, communities, institutions, and society? Topics may include work, economics, culture, politics, law, relationships, inequality, democracy, social institutions, public policy, and the broader consequences of AI for the human future. AI, Leadership, Strategy, and Governance How should leaders make decisions in an AI-rich environment? This track welcomes work addressing leadership, organizational strategy, institutional transformation, governance, policy, risk, workforce development, and responsible AI adoption. AI, Research, Discovery, and Innovation How is AI transforming the process of discovery and the creation of new knowledge? This track includes AI-enabled research, interdisciplinary research methods, scientific discovery, innovation, entrepreneurship, and emerging approaches to scholarship and creative inquiry. SUBMISSION GUIDELINES Please include: • Presentation title • A 250-500-word abstract outlining the topic, approach, and main contribution of the proposed presentation • Preferred conference track • Presenter name(s) and institutional or professional affiliation, if applicable • Contact email(s) • Whether you plan to read a paper or give a presentation using slides A full paper or slide deck is not required at the proposal stage. Email proposals by March 5, 2027, to either conference co-organizer: Dr. Andrew Lang Dean, College of Science and Engineering Senior Professor of Mathematics Oral Roberts University alang@oru.edu Dr. Mark Hall Dean, J.D. McKean Library Senior Professor of English Oral Roberts University mhall@oru.edu Proposals will be reviewed as they are received. Early submissions are encouraged. PRESENTATION FORMAT All presentations will be delivered in person. Standard sessions allow 15 minutes for presentation followed by 5 minutes for questions and discussion. Accepted abstracts will be included in the online conference program. The conference will not publish formal proceedings or full papers. REGISTRATION Registration is required for all attendees, including accepted presenters. Please consult the conference website for registration information, hotel recommendations, schedule updates, and additional details. FEATURED SPEAKERS Orson Scott Card Award-winning author of Ender's Game and Speaker for the Dead. Pat Gelsinger Executive chair and head of technology at Gloo, general partner at Playground Global, and former CEO of Intel and VMware. His career spans more than 45 years in engineering and technology leadership. Joan Slonczewski, PhD Award-winning science fiction author and Professor of Biology at Kenyon College. Their novels include A Door into Ocean, Brain Plague, The Highest Frontier, and Minds in Transit. Their work explores evolution, biotechnology, artificial intelligence, and the future of intelligent life. Ben John, PhD Chief Technology Officer of Digital Turbine and former Vice President of Engineering at Microsoft AI, where he led the Copilot data platform. He previously served as CTO of AppNexus and Xandr. We are imagining more than the future of AI. We are imagining who we will become. Come imagine it with us in Tulsa. Conference website: https://oru.edu/academics/cose/ai-and-the-imagination/

items.title: Inclusion in Motion: Rethinking Policy and Pedagogy in Latin American and Caribbean Classrooms, Thirty Years on from Salamanca
items.excerpt: Introduction Thirty years on from the Salamanca Statement and Framework for Action on Special Needs Education (UNESCO, 1994), Latin America and the Caribbean have gone through a complex and challenging process towards building inclusive education systems. The region's normative frameworks and public policies have incorporated the principles of inclusive e...
items.fullDescription: Introduction Thirty years on from the Salamanca Statement and Framework for Action on Special Needs Education (UNESCO, 1994), Latin America and the Caribbean have gone through a complex and challenging process towards building inclusive education systems. The region's normative frameworks and public policies have incorporated the principles of inclusive education to varying degrees, while curricular and pedagogical practices in classrooms continue to face tensions between the normative mandate and the actual conditions of implementation. This special issue of RECAP: Research in Education Curriculum and Pedagogy invites academics, researchers and teams to submit papers that critically examine the progress made, the challenges that persist and, in particular, what works in relation to inclusive education, special education and public policy in Latin American and Caribbean. Aim of the special issue To bring together original and rigorous research that provides evidence on the curricular and pedagogical transformations driven by inclusive education policy frameworks in Latin America and the Caribbean since 1994, with particular attention to practices, strategies and interventions that have demonstrated positive and sustainable outcomes. RECAP is part of AT-Journals (https://at-journals.com/). The guidelines for authors are available here (https://recap.at-journals.com/recap/index.php/description/about/submissions). Thematic areas Contributions are invited on, among others, the following themes: Normative frameworks and public policy on inclusive education and special education in the region. Policy implementation processes: gaps between normative design and classroom practice. Curricular transformations aimed at inclusion: universal design for learning, curricular adaptations and pedagogical flexibilisation. Initial and continuing teacher education for attending to diversity. Experiences and evidence on effective pedagogical practices (what works) in inclusive contexts. Inclusive education in rural contexts, indigenous peoples, Afro-descendant communities and migration. Family and community participation in inclusive education processes. Evaluation and monitoring of inclusion policies: indicators, information systems and accountability. Comparative studies across countries in the region. Perspectives of students with special educational needs, disabilities and intersecting identities on their own educational trajectories. Types of contributions Empirical research articles, systematic literature reviews, case studies and public policy analyses will be accepted. Manuscripts must comply with RECAP's editorial guidelines. Languages Manuscripts are accepted in Spanish* and English. *Spanish manuscripts will require - in an addition - an English abstract of 300-500 words. items.title: Resonances and Polysemy: Musical Forms and Meanings in the Literary Text.
items.excerpt: Between XVII.34 (2027): Resonances and Polysemy: Musical Forms and Meanings in the Literary Text. Editors : Stefano Franceschini (Roma Tre University), Fiorenzo Iuliano (University of Cagliari) Submission Deadline: 27 May 2027 Publication Date: 15 December 2027 In Chapter 25 of Thomas Mann's Doctor Faustus (1947), Mephistopheles promises the protagonist,...
items.fullDescription: Between XVII.34 (2027): Resonances and Polysemy: Musical Forms and Meanings in the Literary Text. Editors : Stefano Franceschini (Roma Tre University), Fiorenzo Iuliano (University of Cagliari) Submission Deadline: 27 May 2027 Publication Date: 15 December 2027 In Chapter 25 of Thomas Mann's Doctor Faustus (1947), Mephistopheles promises the protagonist, Adrian Leverkühn, twenty-four years of uninterrupted musical creativity in exchange for his soul, assuring him that he will "in drunken indulgence taste every bliss of almost intolerable infusion" and that, "in certain wanton moments," he may "plainly and honestly deem himself a god." Attracted yet alarmed by such an offer, the young composer asks to know the details of the transaction. Mephistopheles replies: "You would have knowledge of the pernicies, of the confutatio? […] one may use and fashion a great many words, yet all of them are but representative, stand for names that do not exist, can make no claim to designate that which can never ever be designated and denounced in words. That is the secret delight and security of hell, that it cannot be denounced, that it lies hidden from language." The devil refers to the inadequacy of language when faced with something as elusive as the essence of hell. The same can be said of music as the art of the ineffable, as Augusto Romano defines it in Musica e psiche (2021). Too often, however, the ineffable tends to be equated with the meaningless, what cannot convey any meaning at all: music, in other words, would possess no expressive means beyond a recursive exercise in self-reference (Hanslick 1854). This perspective, confining musical meaning within the boundaries of the work itself, has been challenged by approaches emphasizing music's capacity to produce historical and cultural meanings that cannot be reduced to formal principles alone (Kramer 2001). Yet one need only consider artistic practices such as program music and film scores, the entire range of discourses centered on music - from interpretive analysis and aesthetic-philosophical treatises to reviews and literary works - as well as the far more subjective experiences of musical transport, whether emotional, imaginative, or synesthetic, which have also been widely debated, to see how difficult it is to sustain the understanding of music as a system characterized by mere semio-phenomenal processes. Although its roots lie in a much older tradition, the relationship between literature and music acquired renewed prominence with modernism, on both the thematic and formal levels. Literature, and fiction in particular, increasingly turned to music as a thematic and structural model (Bucknell 2001; Wolf 1999). If, on the one hand, technological and industrial innovations around the turn of the twentieth century profoundly transformed access to music in domestic spaces - through the spread first of the phonograph and subsequently of radio (Sterne 2003), later leading to modern sound reproduction systems - on the other, the expansion of increasingly noisy urban environments had a sociocultural impact that over time radically reshaped individual acoustic experience (Schafer 1977). Many writers have consequently devoted considerable attention to sound, and particularly to music, as a vehicle for aesthetic, historical, and cultural reflection: from E.T.A. Hoffmann's "Ritter Gluck" (1809) and Honoré de Balzac's "Gambara" (1837), through Lev Tolstoy's Krejcerova sonata (1889), E.M. Forster's Howards End (1910), Aldous Huxley's Point Counter Point (1928), and Mann's aforementioned Doctor Faustus , to Marguerite Duras's Moderato cantabile (1958), Alejo Carpentier's Concierto barroco (1974), Thomas Bernhard's Der Untergeher (1983), Pascal Quignard's Tous les matins du monde (1991), Toni Morrison's Jazz (1992), Roberto Controneo's Presto con fuoco (1995), Vikram Seth's An Equal Music (1999), Richard Powers's The Time of Our Singing (2003), Moisés Kaufman's 33 Variations (2007), Claudio Morandini's Rapsodia su un solo tema. Colloqui con Rafail Dvoinikov (2010), Mathias Énard's Compass (2017), and Jenny Erpenbeck's Kairos (2021), to name but a few. What strategies can a written text employ to represent music? Can a literary text identify and illuminate a network of musical meanings? To what extent can different literary forms - narrative, poetry, and drama - incorporate such meanings into their structures and distinctive expressive modes, making music available to characters and other textual components as a means through which to reflect upon and intervene in reality? This issue of Between aims to explore the forms and modes through which literature, in its various expressions - fiction, poetry, and drama - engages with music, understood not simply as a theme or object of representation, but as a language, a means of knowledge, and a potential principle of formal organization. How does a literary text evoke, rework, recode, or reconstruct musical experience? How can it incorporate musical syntax - rhythm, melody, harmony, tonality, forms, and compositional procedures - and turn it into a means of producing new meanings? From this perspective, the relationship between music and literature may be approached on formal and aesthetic as well as historical, social, and political grounds. Music can contribute to the construction of subjectivities and identities; organize temporality and memory; define generational, cultural, or national affiliations; shape space and everyday experience; or provide a terrain on which the literary text can reflect upon its own limits and its expressive and epistemological possibilities. At the same time, the encounter between word and music raises broader questions concerning intersemiotic translation, intermediality, and the relationships between different systems of signification. The issue welcomes theoretical and methodological contributions as well as studies devoted to individual authors, works, or corpora, with particular emphasis on comparative approaches. Proposals that combine formal analysis with attention to the specific historical, cultural, and media conditions within which musical experience is produced, received, and reworked are especially welcome. Possible areas of inquiry include, but are not limited to: - music as a means for the production and articulation of meaning in literary texts; - musical forms, structures, and practices in the construction of literary texts: rhythmic organization, counterpoint, polyphony, variation, thematic development, serialism, and improvisation; - forms and functions of composition, performance, and listening in literary texts; - music, memory, and affect; - music as a means of interpreting historical, social, and political processes; - technologies of musical composition, recording, reproduction, and circulation and their interaction with literature; - voice and vocality between literature and music; - intersemiotic translation, intermediality, musical ineffability, and the limits of verbal representation. Authors are invited to consult the selected bibliography provided at the end of the call for papers. For questions or further information, please contact the editors at the email addresses ( stefano.franceschini@uniroma3.it and iuliano@unica.it ). Articles ready for publication, not exceeding 40,000 characters including spaces and formatted according to the provided template, with title, abstract, and metadata in English, must be submitted to the journal by 27 May 2027 , following the instructions available on the Submissions page of the Between website (Please note that the Between Journal website is currently under maintenance. Further submission details will be available starting in November 2026). Accepted articles will be published on 15 December 2027 . Contributions are accepted in Italian, English, and French, as well as in bilingual versions. Submissions in a language other than Italian, or in a bilingual version in which one of the languages is English or French, are particularly welcome and encouraged. Selected Bibliography: Bernhart, Walter, Steven Paul Scher, and Werner Wolf, eds. Word and Music Studies: Defining the Field . Amsterdam and Atlanta: Rodopi, 1999. Bucknell, Brad. Literary Modernism and Musical Aesthetics: Pater, Pound, Joyce and Stein . Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2001. Gracyk, Theodore, and Andrew Kania, eds. The Routledge Companion to Philosophy and Music. London and New York: Routledge, 2011. Hanslick, Eduard. The Beautiful in Music: A Contribution to the Revisal of Musical Aesthetics. Trans. by Gustav Cohen. London: Novello and Company, 1891 [1854]. Isacoff, Stuart. Temperament: How Music Became a Battleground for the Great Minds of Western Civilization . New York: Vintage, 2003. Kramer, Lawrence. Musical Meaning: Toward a Critical History. Berkeley and Los Angeles: University of California Press, 2001. Macedo, Frederico. "Space as Metaphor: The Use of Spatial Metaphors in Music and Music Writing." Signata. Annales des sémiotiques / Annals of Semiotics 6 (2015). Messiaen, Olivier. Music and Color: Conversations with Claude Samuel . Portland, OR: Amadeus Press, 1994. Pennacchia, Maddalena. "Intermedialità letteraria. Note sul nomadismo mediatico della letteratura." In Il testo oltre i confini: Passaggi, scambi, migrazioni , edited by Lucia Perrone Capano. Bari: Palomar, 2009. Petermann, Emily. The Musical Novel: Imitation of Musical Structure, Performance, and Reception in Contemporary Fiction . Rochester, NY: Camden House, 2014. Rajewsky, Irina O. "Intermediality, Intertextuality, and Remediation: A Literary Perspective on Intermediality." Intermédialités: Histoire et théorie des arts, des lettres et des techniques 6 (2005). Romano, Augusto. Musica e psiche. Milan: Raffaello Cortina Editore, 2021. Scher, Steven Paul. "Notes toward a Theory of Verbal Music." Comparative Literature 22, no. 2 (1970): 147-56. Smith, Hazel. The Contemporary Literature-Music Relationship: Intermedia, Voice, Technology, Cross-Cultural Exchange . London and New York: Routledge, 2016. Varèse, Edgard. items.title: Classical Echoes: Performing the Influence of Ancient Greek and Roman Literature
items.excerpt: Special Issue Website: https://www.mdpi.com/journal/literature/special_issues/B781Q58SAM Dear Colleagues, This Special Issue of Literature will collect essays addressing the reception, influence, adaptation, or incorporation of literature from the Greco-Roman world into later theatre, film, and television. The Greeks and Romans pioneered a wide range of p...
items.fullDescription: Special Issue Website: https://www.mdpi.com/journal/literature/special_issues/B781Q58SAM Dear Colleagues, This Special Issue of Literature will collect essays addressing the reception, influence, adaptation, or incorporation of literature from the Greco-Roman world into later theatre, film, and television. The Greeks and Romans pioneered a wide range of performed literary styles like tragic and comic drama, or epic and lyric poetry, as well as developing extensive mythic story networks and what we now recognize as formal histories, etc. Some of these works remain among the most influential and beloved writings ever produced by humanity. Because Greco-Roman literature is so culturally powerful and beloved, receptions and uses of it have occurred continually since the Greco-Roman era itself, in myriad different ways. This Issue seeks articles focused on performed receptions, exploring the cultural and artistic politics of how Greco-Roman material is brought to life for viewers, either on stages or screens. The recent controversies about casting and "historical accuracy" with Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey film remind us of the power and perils of live performance in the evocation of classics, so the articles for this Issue will interrogate the weight of and responses to classics' cultural authority. The Special Issue aims to provide current scholarly arguments about the role and ongoing power of Greek and Roman literature in theatre, film, television, or other performed media, consistent with the broader aims and scope of Literature. Purposefully taking a broad lens, the Issue seeks essays focused across time periods (e.g., medieval to the present), different national or regional performances/arts, and across media in order to bring together the most comprehensive body of essays possible. Potential topics include, but are not limited to: Theatrical or performed adaptation of or allusions to Greek and Roman literature within the Greco-Roman world. Medieval European or Middle Eastern reworkings and influence of Greco-Roman poetry or drama. Renaissance or Enlightenment re-conceptualizations of classical works. Re-writings, reworkings, artistic depictions, stagings, etc., of Greek or Roman literature for popular audiences (including Nolan's recent film). Global receptions and performances of Greco-Roman literature for postcolonial or comparative literature purposes. Feminist performed engagement with and critique of classics. Dr. Phillip Zapkin Guest Editor Manuscript Submission Information Manuscripts should be submitted online at www.mdpi.com by registering and logging in to this website. Once you are registered, click here to go to the submission form. Manuscripts can be submitted until the deadline. All submissions that pass pre-check are peer-reviewed. Accepted papers will be published continuously in the journal (as soon as accepted) and will be listed together on the special issue website. Research articles, review articles as well as short communications are invited. For planned papers, a title and short abstract (about 250 words) can be sent to the Editorial Office for assessment. Submitted manuscripts should not have been published previously, nor be under consideration for publication elsewhere (except conference proceedings papers). All manuscripts are thoroughly refereed through a double-anonymized peer-review process. A guide for authors and other relevant information for submission of manuscripts is available on the Instructions for Authors page. Literature is an international peer-reviewed open access quarterly journal published by MDPI. Please visit the Instructions for Authors page before submitting a manuscript. The Article Processing Charge (APC) for publication in this open access journal is 1000 CHF (Swiss Francs). Submitted papers should be well formatted and use good English. Authors may use MDPI's English editing service prior to publication or during author revisions. Keywords: Greek Roman literature reception adaptation studies classics
